title_original: In Search of the Future, Artists Give New Life to Dead AI Models
editorial_title_zh: 在对未来的寻觅中，艺术家为死去的AI模型注入新生
editorial_excerpt_zh: 生成式AI文生视频模型的飞速发展催生了旧金山tiat画廊的新展“后代”（Post Generation）。

"https://www.artnews.com/t/link-rot/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "过去几年间，生成式AI文生视频模型的发展一直通过一个简单的提示词来记录：“威尔·史密斯吃通心粉”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第一批视频发布于2023年，使用的是新发布的Stable Diffusion模型，展现了该演员狼吞虎咽、面目狰狞的渲染形象：他用双手把一团通心粉状的斑块塞进嘴里，而通心粉却随即滑落、变形、拉伸、与周围的伪影融为一体，或者直接消失。在三年内，这项测试几乎达到了其终点，通心粉对重力做出自然反应，并与场景中的其他物体——叉子、盘子和史密斯的嘴——进行了正确的交互。但是，随着每一个新模型以不间断的节奏接踵而至，那些在此之前问世的模型，或者在它们训练期间生成的视频，都遭遇了什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正是这个问题驱动了旧金山tiat画廊的新展“后代”（Post Generation）。三位艺术家对由Veo 1生成的视频档案进行了反思，Veo 1是谷歌于2024年开发、现已停用的模型。该模型仅发布供内部使用，尽管最终遭到泄露，但它似乎几乎无法正常运行。它只能生成六秒钟的视频，生成之间需要漫长的等待，并产生可预见的超现实结果：一匹六条腿的马在湿润的草地上驰骋，一团可能是儿童在落叶堆中玩耍的静电污迹，以及一个在水池里游泳的三肢古人类。在模型被关闭并被先后发布的公开模型Veo 2和Veo 3取代之前，研究人员生成了数十万段视频。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“由于这些模型消耗极大的资源，且每一个新模型都更快、更高效，因此很难证明保留旧模型的合理性。没有人能够使用Veo1进行生成，它所产出的结果也并未公开，”谷歌创意实验室（Google’s Creative Lab）的高级创意技术专家、该展的组织者蒂娜·塔里吉安（Tina Tarighian）说道。“所以我想，我们能用这些模型的剩余残片做些什么？我们能把这个档案赠予艺术家吗？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "塔里吉安将档案的一部分分享给了编舞家泽莉亚·ZZ·谭（Zelia ZZ Tan）、创意工程师卡琳·中村（Karyn Nakamura）和纤维艺术家海莉·莫丁（Haley Mortin），并邀请每人以新作品作出回应。由此产生的展览是对该技术本质的多媒体沉思，也是其发展特定时刻的档案。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/pg-2.jpeg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "海莉·莫丁、蒂娜·塔里吉安、泽莉亚·ZZ·谭和卡琳·中村。", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对莫丁而言，使用这些训练数据是她艺术实践的自然延伸，她的创作将AI生成的图像、源自研究论文的图像以及其他AI伪影融入针织作品中。她对这些伪影的着迷部分源于她曾担任数据标注员的前一份工作，这是一种往往隐形的体力劳动，全球各地的工人在其中对图像进行分类和加标签，以教导AI模型“看到”并正确识别物体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“那是2018年，我刚从大学毕业，我不知道什么是AI，我需要钱，”莫丁说。“我以为这只是一份数据录入工作。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在接下来的两年里，莫丁发现自己不仅要解决验证码（CAPTCHA）测试并根据图像包含的物体和主题对图像进行标注，还要根据更为主观的类别进行标注，例如她认为照片中的人在表达什么情绪。Veo 1的产出虽然是间接的，但也是这种劳动的产品。在审视这些产出时，莫丁决定专注于模型生成的奇异文字形式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“它产生了两种风格的胡言乱语，即这些字形般的形状或空洞的短语，”莫丁说。“这些[视觉]模型不像LLM（大语言模型）那样学习文本，相反，它们把文本作为一种纹理来学习。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这促使莫丁思考18世纪女性制作的刺绣样品。许多年轻女性初次接触文字不是通过墨水和纸张，而是通过刺绣。当她们练习缝制文字时，常常利用这些样品来记录家族历史。莫丁由此创作的作品《汤由水制成（10个样品）》（Soup Is Made of Water (10 Samplers), 2026）由十件针织作品组成，捕捉了Veo 1生成的不同形式的乱码文本，反思了文本生产的历史以及保存和归档这些文本的实践。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些作品采用黑白纱线渲染，描绘了一个循环的涂鸦、一个试图拼写出（也许是）“美丽”[b eurt]的颤动书法字体，以及一个只能被描述为通常刺在布鲁克林里奇伍德（Ridgewood）大腿上的那种符文纹理的刺青。该作品巧妙地将语言学习和历史构建的不同实践联系起来并加以颠覆：18世纪女性的实践、当代机器的实践，以及试图处理和记录机器训练的艺术家的实践。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卡琳·中村也接受了塔里吉安的邀请，探索Veo 1及其他生成模型背后的研究历史，并在单一作品中结合了多种视频技术。在《光之劳作》（Labor of Light, 2016）中，一系列技术汇聚在一起，成为一座献给视频制作历史的某种圣坛。一个白色装置悬挂在一对缆绳上，发出对观众来说看似稳定但其闪烁中包含着《眨眼之间》（Quicker ’n a Wink, 1940）模拟信号的光束，这是一部解释麻省理工学院（MIT）的哈罗德·埃杰顿（Harold Edgerton）如何开发用于制作慢动作镜头的告诉摄影技术的电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这束光线投射到一个投影仪上，将由 Veo 1 生成的视频拼贴投影到白色的布上，每个剪辑片段都从一片鲜艳色彩的静态干扰场中浮现。中村使用了 RGB 噪点——这是生成式人工智能的一个关键组成部分，图像和视频正是从最初的噪点场中生成的。在白布下方，用油灰固定的细小牙签支撑着几篇具有里程碑意义的研究论文的打印件，这些论文推进了现代人工智能生成背后的技术，其中包括扩散模型。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我觉得图像制作的过程、视频以及视频系统的过程美得不可思议，其中蕴含着大量的工艺，”中村说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管有人能在这类技术中发现美，但中村仍担忧发展速度正使得其内部运作原理越来越难以理解，从而限制了人们在当代图像制作过程中进行创造性干预和发挥能动性的能力。出于这个原因，她的作品常常驻足于早期模型（如 Stable Diffusion 1.5）的故障与空白之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“因为我喜欢 Stable Diffusion 1.5，有时我会想：‘噢，我是不是在当卢德分子？’”中村沉思道，“‘比如，现在到底什么才算进步？’\"", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在日益病态的现实与未来结果的背景下，这些艺术家们正审视着一项尽管问世仅短短几年却正以惊人速度推进的技术。然而，在将进步等同于永恒加速的文化中，稍作停顿就意味着面临被淘汰的风险。编舞家 Zelia ZZ Tan 在 10 月 8 日展览开幕式上表演的一场十分钟的舞蹈中探讨了这种张力。这场表演将编舞与动画虚拟形象相结合，捕捉了 Veo 1 视频中身体移动和手势的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当我开始意识到生成的身体、物理身体以及计算身体之间存在许多相似之处，并且在它们如何表现方面也存在许多规则时，我是通过动作而不是仅通过文字来搜寻这个档案的，”Tan 说道。但与生成身体的运动局限性共舞需要脆弱感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tan 接着说道：“拥有一个身体、能够亲临现场是如此荣幸，也许我展现出的并非训练最为扎实的技巧，但去倾听、在舞台上表现出迟疑、等待某件事情发生——这正是身为表演者亲临现场力量的一部分。”", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot , a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet. The column will appear every other Monday.

The development of generative AI text-to-video models has been charted over the past few years through a simple prompt: “Will Smith eating pasta.”

The first videos, posted in 2023 using newly released Stable Diffusion models, feature a ravenous, monstrous rendering of the actor shoveling a pasta-shaped blob into his mouth with his hands, only for it to slide, morph, stretch, merge with surrounding artifacts, or simply disappear. Within three years, the test has nearly reached its endpoint, with the pasta responding naturally to gravity and interacting correctly with the other objects in the scene: the fork, the plate, and Smith’s mouth. But as each new model arrives in relentless succession, what happens to those that came before it, or to the videos produced during their training?

That question drives “Post Generation,” a new exhibition at tiat gallery in San Francisco. Three artists reflect on a video archive generated by Veo 1, a now-defunct model developed by Google in 2024. Released only for internal use, though eventually leaked, the model seemed barely functional. It could produce only six-second videos, with long waits between generations and predictably surreal results: a six-legged horse galloping across a wet field, a staticky smudge that might be children playing in a pile of leaves, and a three-limbed hominid swimming in a pool. Researchers generated hundreds of thousands of videos before the model was shut down and superseded by successive generations, Veo 2 and Veo 3, both of which were released to the public.

“Because these models are so resource intensive and because each new model is faster and more efficient, it’s hard to justify keeping old models around. No one can generate using Veo1, and the outputs it produced aren’t publicly available,” said Tina Tarighian, a senior creative technologist at Google’s Creative Lab and the show’s organizer. “So I thought, what can we do with these leftover scraps of a model? Can we gift this archive to artists?”

Tarighian shared a portion of the archive with choreographer Zelia ZZ Tan, creative engineer Karyn Nakamura, and fiber artist Haley Mortin, asking each to respond with new work. The resulting exhibition is a multimedia meditation on the nature of this technology and an archive of a particular moment in its development.

For Mortin, working with this training data was a natural extension of her practice, which incorporates AI-generated images, images sourced from research papers, and other AI artifacts into knit works. Her fascination with these artifacts stems in part from a former job as a data annotator, a form of often-invisible human labor in which workers around the world categorize and tag images to teach AI models to “see” and correctly identify objects.

“It was 2018, I had just graduated college, I didn’t know what AI was, and I needed money,” said Mortin. “I thought it was just a data entry job.”

Over the next two years, Mortin found herself solving CAPTCHA tests and labeling images not only by the objects and subjects they contained but also by more subjective categories, such as the emotion she thought a person in a photo was expressing. The Veo 1 outputs are, albeit indirectly, a product of this kind of labor. In examining them, Mortin decided to focus on the strange forms of text the model generated.

“It produced two flavors of nonsense, these glyph-like shapes or empty phrases,” said Mortin. “These [visual] models don’t learn text like an LLM [large language model] does, rather, they learn text as a texture.”

This led Mortin to consider the embroidery samplers made by women in the 18th century. Many young women first encountered writing not through ink and paper but through embroidery. As they practiced stitching text, they often used these samplers to record family histories. Mortin’s resulting work, Soup Is Made of Water (10 Samplers) (2026), comprises ten knitted pieces that capture the different forms of garbled text generated by Veo 1, reflecting on the histories of text production and the practices through which it is preserved and archived.

Rendered in black and white yarn, the pieces depict a looping scribble, a calligraphic font attempting to spell, perhaps, “beauty” [b eurt], and what can only be described as a sigil tattoo of the kind commonly inked on thighs in Ridgewood, Brooklyn. The work deftly brings into conversation, and inverts, different practices of language learning and history-making: those of 18th-century women, contemporary machines, and artists attempting to process and document a machine’s training.

Karyn Nakamura also took up Tarighian’s invitation to explore the research histories behind Veo 1 and other generative models, combining several video technologies in a single work. In Labor of Light (2016), an assemblage of technologies comes together as a kind of altar to the history of video production. Suspended from a pair of cables, a white device emits a beam of light that appears stable to the viewer but contains, in its flicker, the analog signal of Quicker ’n a Wink (1940), a film explaining how MIT’s Harold Edgerton developed the high-speed photography technology used to produce slow-motion footage.

The beam of light leads down to a projector that casts a collage of Veo 1-generated videos onto a white cloth, each clip emerging from a static-like field of vivid colors. Nakamura uses RGB noise, a key component of generative AI, in which images and videos are generated from an initial field of noise. Beneath the cloth, small toothpicks held in place with putty support printouts of landmark research papers that advanced the techniques behind modern AI generation, including diffusion.

“I find the process of image making and the process of video and video systems incredibly beautiful, there’s a lot of craft in there,” said Nakamura.

Even as someone who sees beauty in these technologies, Nakamura worries that the pace of development makes their inner workings increasingly difficult to understand, limiting people’s ability to intervene creatively and exercise agency in contemporary image-making processes. For this reason, her work often dwells in the glitches and gaps of earlier models, such as Stable Diffusion 1.5.

“Because I like Stable Diffusion 1.5, sometimes I think, ‘Oh, am I being a Luddite?’” Nakamura mused. “Like, what is even progress right now?”

Against a backdrop of increasingly morbid present and future outcomes, these artists reckon with a technology advancing at breakneck speed despite being barely a few years old. Yet in a culture that equates progress with perpetual acceleration, to pause is to risk obsolescence. Choreographer Zelia ZZ Tan explores this tension in a ten-minute dance performed at the exhibition’s opening on October 8. Combining choreography with animated avatars, the performance captures the ways bodies move and gesture in Veo 1 videos.

“I searched the archive through movement rather than only through words when I started to realize that between generated bodies, physical bodies, and the computational body, there are a lot of similarities and also a lot of rules based on how they can perform,” said Tan. But dancing with the limitation of movement of the generated body required vulnerability.

Tan continued: “It’s such an honor to have a body, to be able to be present there, and maybe I’m not showing the most trained technique, but to listen, to be hesitant on stage, to wait for something to happen – that’s part of the power of being there as a performer.”
excerpt_original: The breakneck development of generative AI text-to-video models drives “Post Generation,” a new exhibition at tiat gallery in San Francisco.

translated_excerpt_zh: 生成式人工智能文本到视频模型的飞速发展推动了旧金山 tiat 画廊的新展览“后一代”。

article_text:
O Festival ZUM 2026 acontecerá nos dias 7 e 8 de novembro , no IMS Paulista.

O Festival ZUM é um evento que a revista ZUM promove anualmente em torno da fotografia e da cultura visual contemporânea, com debates, oficinas, exposições e feira de fotolivros. Confira abaixo a programação completa do festival.

SÁBADO, 7 de novembro

10h: Abertura, conversa e anúncio dos premiados da Convocatória de Fotolivros 2026 / Biblioteca. Autores e editores apresentam as publicações selecionadas. Entrada gratuita, por ordem de chegada. Lugares limitados.

13h-20h: Exposição da Convocatória de Fotolivros ZUM / IMS / Biblioteca Entrada gratuita, por ordem de chegada. Lugares limitados.

10h-18h: Feira & Lançamentos de Fotolivros / Térreo. Conheça os participantes. Entrada gratuita.

14h-20h: Instalação Doze flechas feitas de água , de Inaê Moreira / Foyer do teatro

CONVERSAS / Cinema

Evento ao vivo com interpretação em Libras (Língua Brasileira de Sinais)

Da série Doze flechas feitas de água , de Inaê Moreira, 2026

Marina de Jesus , da série Esmeraldas não é Cohab porque tem elevador , de Renan Teles, 2026

Valentina Tong

14h30 – Habitar territórios

Doze flechas feitas de água , performance de Inaê Moreira Renan Teles + Valentina Tong + Inaê Moreira

Mediação de Rony Maltz

As disputas urbanas, ambientais e históricas unem os retratos de moradores da periferia de São Paulo feitos por Renan Teles , a destruição das montanhas capixabas pela indústria de pedras ornamentais documentada por Valentina Tong e as conexões transatlânticas entre Salvador e Benin evocadas pela obra de Inaê Moreira .

Entrada gratuita, sujeita à lotação do espaço. Distribuição de senhas para qualquer uma das mesas da programação do dia, a partir das 12h na Limite de 1 senha por pessoa.

Paula Sampaio

Antônio Gaudério

17h – Memórias urgentes

Paula Sampaio + Ana Aurora Borges/Acervo Antonio Gaudério

Mediação de Marlene Bergamo

A fotógrafa Paula Sampaio apresenta registros das populações amazônicas e de seus conflitos feitos ao longo de décadas vivendo em Belém, enquanto Ana Aurora Borges narra o desafio de preservar a obra do pai, o premiado fotojornalista Antônio Gaudério, que perdeu a memória após um acidente.

Entrada gratuita, sujeita à lotação do espaço. Distribuição de senhas para qualquer uma das mesas da programação do dia, a partir das 12h na Limite de 1 senha por pessoa.

19h – Ritual e revolução

Carrie Mae Weems com Aldeide Delgado e Daniele Queiroz

Um dos principais nomes da arte contemporânea mundial, Carrie Mae Weems apresenta 40 anos de trabalho, em que utiliza a fotografia para discutir poder, identidade e ativismo. Parceria: Women Photographers International Archive (WOPHA).

Entrada gratuita, sujeita à lotação do espaço. Distribuição de senhas para qualquer uma das mesas da programação do dia, a partir das 12h na Limite de 1 senha por pessoa.

DOMINGO, 8 de novembro

10h-20h: Doze flechas feitas de água , instalação de Inaê Moreira / Foyer do cinema

10h-18h: Feira e lançamentos de fotolivros / Térreo

10h-20h: Exposição da Convocatória de Fotolivros ZUM / IMS / Biblioteca

11h: Mulheres na fotografia das Américas , conversa com Aldeide Delgado e Daniele Queiroz / Biblioteca

Aldeide Delgado , fundadora da Women Photographers International Archive (WOPHA) e Daniele Queiroz , curadora de Arte Contemporânea do Instituto Moreira Salles, conversam sobre os desafios enfrentados por mulheres no circuito da fotografia, destacando iniciativas de coletivos e artistas no continente americano. A conversa será em espanhol. Parceria: Women Photographers International Archive/WOPHA.

Entrada gratuita, por ordem de chegada. Lugares limitados. Evento ao vivo com interpretação em Libras (Língua Brasileira de Sinais)

OFICINA

10h30-12h30 Oficina: Publicações possíveis , com Arturo Salazar e José Ruiz (Ediciones Réplica) / sala de aula – 2º andar

Os fundadores da Ediciones Réplica — editora colombiana que publica livros de arte e fotografia sobretudo a partir do trabalho com arquivos — convidam os participantes a criar, editar e produzir uma publicação colaborativa, explorando conceitos e técnicas com os recursos disponíveis. A oficina será em espanhol

Entrada gratuita. Lugares limitados Distribuição de senhas 30 minutos antes do evento Limite de uma senha por pessoa Evento ao vivo com interpretação em Libras (Língua Brasileira de Sinais)

CONVERSAS / Cinema

Evento ao vivo com interpretação em Libras (Língua Brasileira de Sinais)

Lia D Castro

Manaura Clandestina

15h – Corpos em disputa

Lia D Castro + Manaura Clandestina

Mediação de Cinthia Marcelle

Com polaróides e fotos de celulares, Lia D Castro usa a prostituição e a fotografia para investigar o ódio e o desejo, a masculinidade e a branquitude, enquanto Manaura Clandestina constrói um arquivo que celebra o cotidiano e a comunidade travesti ao seu redor.

Entrada gratuita, sujeita à lotação do espaço. Distribuição de senhas para qualquer uma das mesas da programação do dia, a partir das 12h na Limite de 1 senha por pessoa.

Frame do filme Mato seco em chamas , de Adirley Queirós e Joana Pimenta

Frame do filme Que horas ela volta? , de Anna Muylaert

17h – Democracia em movimento

Adirley Queirós + Anna Muylaert

Mediação de Mariana Queen Nwabasili

Diretores de filmes como Que horas ela volta? (2015) e Mato seco em chamas (2023), Anna Muylaert e Adirley Queirós conversam sobre a responsabilidade do cinema em narrar a história direta do Brasil para fortalecer visões de mundo mais democráticas e igualitárias.

Entrada gratuita, sujeita à lotação do espaço. Distribuição de senhas para qualquer uma das mesas da programação do dia, a partir das 12h na Limite de 1 senha por pessoa.

CONVIDADOS

Adirley Queirós (Morro Agudo de Goiás, GO, 1970) é cineasta, graduado em cinema pela UnB e morador de Ceilândia. Realizou os filmes A cidade é uma só? (2012), Era uma vez Brasília (2017) e Mato seco em chamas (2022), entre outros. Branco sai, preto fica (2014) ganhou diversos prêmios, entre eles o de Melhor Filme no Festival de Cinema de Brasília.

Aldeide Delgado (Havana, Cuba, 1983) é historiadora de arte e curadora. Fundou e dirige a Women Photographers International Archive (WOPHA), organização sem fins lucrativos que pesquisa, promove e apoia o papel das mulheres e das pessoas identificadas como não-binárias na fotografia. [Foto: Gaby Ojeda. Cortesia da WOPHA]

Anna Muylaert (São Paulo, SP, 1964) é diretora e roteirista, autora dos filmes Durval Discos (2001) e A melhor mãe do mundo (2025), entre outros. Seu filme Que horas ela volta? (2015) venceu mais de 60 prêmios, entre eles o Prêmio do Público na 65ª Berlinale. É membro da Academia do Oscar.

Ana Aurora Borges (São Paulo, SP, 1994) é produtora cultural e gestora de arte. Formada em letras e comunicação é mestranda em arte e literatura na Universidade Federal de São Paulo. Filha do fotojornalista Antônio Gaudério, atua na preservação e divulgação da obra do pai, que perdeu a memória em um acidente sofrido em 2008.

Carrie Mae Weems (Portland, EUA, 1953) é uma das mais influentes artistas norte-americanas. Ao longo dos últimos 40 anos, construiu uma obra que discute identidade, território, racismo e relações de poder, utilizando fotografias, texto, tecido, áudio, imagens digitais, instalações e vídeo. Recebeu diversos prêmios, entre eles a Bolsa MacArthur Genius e o prêmio pelo conjunto da obra da Fundação Black Caucus do Congresso dos Estados Unidos, em 2013. [Foto: Jerry Klineberg]

Cinthia Marcelle (Belo Horizonte, MG, 1974) é artista visual. Realizou exposições no Museu de Serralves (2025), na Modern Art Oxford (2017) e no MoMA PS1 (2016). Participou da 59ª Carnegie International (2026) e da 57ª Bienal de Veneza (2017) junto com Tiago Mata Machado, recebendo o prêmio de Menção Honrosa. [Foto: Nti Uirá]

Daniele Queiroz (São Paulo, SP, 1986) é curadora de Arte Contemporânea no IMS. Doutoranda e mestra em Arquitetura e Urbanismo pela FAU-USP, foi cocuradora das exposições Zanele Muholi: Beleza Valente e Entre Nós: Dez anos de Bolsa ZUM/IMS . É criadora do projeto A História é Outra , plataforma que pesquisa e difunde o trabalho de mulheres artistas no campo da fotografia. [Foto: Keiny Andrade]

Ediciones Réplica (Colômbia, 2000) é um coletivo independente de pesquisa, edição e curadoria fundado por Arturo Salazar e José Ruiz. O coletivo investiga as histórias e os arquivos da fotografia latino-americana, produzindo publicações, palestras, programas públicos e exposições.

Inaê Moreira (Salvador, BA, 1990) é artista multimídia, diretora e performer, formada em dança pela Universidade Federal da Bahia e mestranda em artes pelo PPGArtes/Uerj. Ganhadora da Bolsa ZUM/IMS 2025, foi destaque da revista ZUM #31. [Foto: João Aleixo]

Lia D Castro (Martinópolis, SP, 1978) é artista visual e escritora. Realizou palestras em Vevey e Lausane, na Suíça. Atualmente desenvolve o projeto Seus Filhos Também Praticam , utilizando sua experiência com a prostituição como ferramenta de investigação sobre raça, classe, gênero e sexualidade.

Manauara Clandestina (Manaus, AM, 1992) é artista, trabalha com performance, música, fotografia, cinema e transmutação têxtil. Foi diretora artística do Ateliê TRANSmoras, ao lado de Vicenta Perrotta. Participou da 60ª Bienal de Veneza (2024), da 36ª Bienal de São Paulo (2025) e da 16ª Bienal de Gwangju. [Foto: José Pelegrini]

Mariana Queen Nwabasili (São Paulo, SP) é jornalista, pesquisadora e curadora-programadora de filmes. Doutoranda e mestra em meios e processos audiovisuais pela ECA/USP e mestra em curadoria cinematográfica pela Elías Querejeta Zine Eskola, na Espanha, programou mostras e festivais como Tiradentes, CineBH, CineOP, Forumdoc.bh, Cabíria e FestCurtasBH.

Marlene Bergamo (São Paulo, SP, 1965) é fotojornalista há 35 anos. Fotografou para os jornais Notícias Populares e Folha de S.Paulo , onde trabalha desde 1995. Coautora dos livros Brasil Bom de Bola (Tempo D’Imagem, 1998) e Carandiru: registro geral (Wide Publishing, 2003). Atua como colaboradora na mídia independente.

Paula Sampaio (Belo Horizonte, MG, 1965) é fotógrafa graduada em comunicação social pela Universidade Federal do Pará (UFPA). Foi repórter fotográfica nos jornais Diário do Pará e O Liberal , entre outros e diretora do Núcleo de Fotografia do Centro de Cultura e Turismo Sesc Ver-o-Peso (2009-2021), em Belém (PA). Foi destaque da revista ZUM #28. [Autorretrato]

Renan Teles (São Paulo, SP, 1986) é fotógrafo e artista multimídia. Participou da 36ª Bienal de São Paulo (2025) com o coletivo Vilanismo. Realizou as exposições Esmeraldas não é Cohab porque tem elevador (2021) no Centro Cultural São Paulo, e Fotografia popular brasileira (2018), na Oficina Cultural Oswald de Andrade, em São Paulo. Foi destaque da revista ZUM #30. [Autorretrato]

Rony Maltz é editor e professor, doutor em linguagens visuais pela EBA/UFRJ e mestre em fotografia pelo Bard College (NY). Criou o selo independente {Lp} press, com Carolina Cattan. Curador da exposição ZineZona (2026), no Instituto Moreira Salles, entre outras. É editor da revista ZUM. [Foto: Dafne Capella]

Valentina Tong (1988) é fotógrafa, arquiteta e curadora. Graduou-se em arquitetura e urbanismo na Escola da Cidade, em São Paulo. Ganhou o prêmio Marc Ferrez de Fotografia com a série Viagem geológica no Seridó Potiguar (2022). Expôs a série Serra da Capivara no Museu Brasileiro da Escultura e da Ecologia, em São Paulo (2023). Foi destaque da revista ZUM #30.

"15世纪和16世纪初的人文主义者面临的一个根本课题是语言问题，彼得罗·本博为此提出了一个既直接又严谨的解决方案：薄伽丘用于散文，彼特拉克的《歌集》（Canzoniere）用于诗歌。本博于1501年为威尼斯历史悠久的阿尔多·马努齐奥印刷所主编了一版《歌集》。这位印刷商制作了一个“可以握在手中”的版本，即八开本，旨在随时随地阅读，因此也适合不仅由学者组成的受众。这种袖珍本直接源自本博的府邸，阿尔多曾在其父贝尔纳多·本博的藏书室里见过小开本的手稿。通过使用斜体字，该印刷所使得该书能够以实用且便携的开本进行复制，从而巩固了本博版《歌集》的成功。自此，“小彼特拉克”成为宫廷中梦寐以求的物件和社交尊贵的标志。", article_text:
Tema fondamentale per gli umanisti del Quattrocento e del primo Cinquecento è la questione della lingua, per cui Pietro Bembo propone una soluzione tanto immediata quanto rigorosa: Boccaccio per la prosa e il Canzoniere di Petrarca per la poesia. Bembo cura nel 1501 un’edizione del Canzoniere per la storica tipografia veneziana di Aldo Manuzio . Il tipografo produce una versione “che si tiene in mano”, ovvero un formato in-ottavo pensato per essere letto ovunque e, dunque, anche accessibile a un pubblico non composto da soli studiosi. L’enchiridio veniva direttamente da casa Bembo, dove Aldo aveva visto dei manoscritti di piccolo formato nella collezione libraria del padre, Bernardo Bembo . Usando la stampa in corsivo, la tipografia rende possibile la riproduzione del volume nel formato pratico e portatile, suggellando il successo dell’edizione bembiana del Canzoniere. Sin da subito il petrarchino diviene un oggetto desiderato a corte e segno di distinzione sociale.

Gli artisti ritraggono innumerevoli nobili riuscendo a inquadrare questa moda dilagante. Tra il 1517 e il 1523, Correggio dipinge Ritratto di uomo che legge : il volumetto che l’uomo tiene in mano è, secondo lo studioso Andrea Muzzi, proprio un petrarchino. Il cervo che emerge dalle fronde boscose sembrerebbe alludere ai sonetti CXC e CCCXIX del Canzoniere . Uno schema simile si riscontra nell’opera Ritratto d’uomo col petrarchino di Parmigianino , del 1524 ca. L’uomo veste tutto di nero, il colore della nobiltà all’epoca, e tiene in mano un petrarchino: il nome del poeta si intravede scritto in oro sulla copertina del libro.

Grazie in particolar modo alle Prose della volgar lingua del 1525, il modello bembiano predomina sugli altri, facendo sì che Petrarca assurga a paradigma esclusivo della lingua poetica. Il repertorio fisso, il monolinguismo, la tendenza alla vaghezza e gli espedienti retorici codificati nel Canzoniere permettono l’accesso alla produzione lirica di sonetti anche a coloro che non sono letterati di mestiere, e per la prima volta anche alle donne.

Tra i celebri personaggi del Cinquecento che partecipano al fenomeno del Petrarchismo vi sono Giovanni della Casa , ritratto da Pontormo , Michelangelo Buonarroti e l’inarrestabile Vittoria Colonna . Il modello proposto da Bembo diviene un’esperienza condivisa da artisti, dame, diplomatici e politici che scrivono poesia, esperienza parte dell’apparato raffinato a cui appartengono e delle convenzioni sociali che condividono. Il sonetto “alla maniera” di Petrarca, oltre a essere una potente esperienza letteraria, assume il carattere di fenomeno sociale.

Anche le nobildonne si faranno rappresentare con il petrarchino, con l’obiettivo di mostrare lo status e il livello culturale. Andrea del Sarto dipinge nel 1528 ca. Dama col petrarchino , in cui la dama rappresentata indica la pagina aperta su due sonetti.

Bronzino ritrae Laura Battiferri con in mano il petrarchino. La poetessa, originaria di Urbino, pubblica la sua produzione già nel 1560 ottenendo riscontri positivi da numerosi letterati del tempo. In questo periodo di fervente attività artistica e intellettuale, il fenomeno del Petrarchismo e la rappresentazione del petrarchino all’interno delle opere sono testimoni del simbiotico rapporto tra il vivere di corte e la produzione artistica. L’occasione per le donne di poter accedere all’attività intellettuale e letteraria ha esiti inaspettati: le voci poetiche sono molte e di valore, circostanza che incentiva la produzione di raccolte e antologie. Nel 1559 Lodovico Domenichi cura la prima raccolta di Rime diverse d’alcune nobilissime et virtuosissime donne .

Domenico Puligo dipinge nel 1523-1525 ca. Ritratto di dama . La donna è probabilmente Barbara Rafficani Salutati , amata da Machiavelli e lodata da Vasari , colta e celebre cortigiana nota per le sue doti come cantante, come attrice e come poetessa. Nel dipinto la donna tiene aperto dinanzi a sé un petrarchino, elemento confermato dalla presenza sul taglio del libro della scritta “PETRARCHA”. Sulle pagine, invece, sono scritti i primi quattro versi del sonetto CCXIII, nel quale Petrarca descrive Laura attraverso i suoi doni e le sue capacità, tra i quali spicca il canto. La dama ha tra le mani un volume di musica.

Mentre il Petrarchismo codifica nei propri testi il modello della dama onesta e incorporea, le donne si fanno rappresentare colte e parte attiva della produzione letteraria riconosciuta e apprezzata dalle corti e dagli intellettuali. Laura è la donna ideale amata dal poeta. Barbara Rafficani Salutati è la donna che si mostra, fiera e consapevole della sua posizione nel mondo e delle sue capacità.

But they’re not allowing themselves to think as far ahead as the Oscars, even as Netflix, with “La Bola Negra” as the crown jewel in its 2026 slate, clearly is."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Javi Ambrossi — I think he’s a witch. We’ll see tomorrow.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For his part, Calvo emphasizes the film’s potential impact — illuminating a story of queer hope during a dark stretch of history, then as now. His ambitions reach beyond the Oscar race. Academy attention, he says, “would be a dream come true, but you should remember why you made the movie. Making the movie was a dream. Everything is a dream. So we just keep dreaming.”"}]
article_text:
For Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau , the romance that fuels “ La Bola Negra ” wasn’t the challenge.

“It wasn’t hard to fall in love with him,” Bernardeau says, looking at his co-star. The two men, both 29-year-old Spaniards, haven’t tired of one another yet, despite a global tour that began in Cannes this spring and has now brought them to New York. “It was hard to create war.”

Related Stories

Tom Skerritt, 'Picket Fences' and 'Alien' Star, Dies at 93

Those two forces, love and war, coexist painfully in what may be the most ambitious film of this year’s Oscar season. Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the two-man team known as Los Javis , “La Bola Negra” depicts the lives of multiple gay men in Spain over three separate timelines: In 1932, young Carlos (Milo Quifes) is blackballed — hence the film’s title — from a social club over his sexuality. In 1937, at the height of the Spanish Civil War, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau play, respectively, a soldier and the prisoner of war he must guard, as their affections blossom inexplicably across political lines. And in 2017, historian Alberto (Carlos González) struggles to figure out how the two preceding tales intersect, stumped until an academic (Glenn Close in a brief, striking cameo) steps in to help.

The story of Spain’s rupture and its fall into repressive dictatorship wasn’t news to the actors. “It’s something that has touched everybody — our great-grandparents were all involved,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “It’s common in our DNA in Spanish society.” But to make the history feel real and immediate, they had to learn how to behave like soldiers. “We received military preparation — how to hold a rifle,” says Guitarricadelafuente, who has a gentle, soft-spoken bearing both in person and onscreen. His Sebastián would rather be playing his trumpet — he fights only reluctantly; he’s more at home in his feelings than in combat. “There’s a naiveness to him,” he continues, “but he’s not stupid. Playing the trumpet is what makes him have hope in the future — one day, he’ll be able to go to Madrid and be a musician.” Indeed, an encounter with a vivacious lounge singer, played by Penélope Cruz, convinces Sebastián that the world is broader than he ever suspected, in a dazzling scene at the heart of the movie.

At least one stakeholder in “La Bola Negra” wanted to be sure Guitarricadelafuente could be credible as a fighter as well as a lover: Meeting him for the first time, Pedro Almodóvar, one of the movie’s producers, asked whether the singer had any edge at all.

Guitarricadelafuente relates Almodóvar’s question first in Spanish before translating it: “Is he gonna avoid just being, like … nice ?”

He’s going to need some armor as he gears up for awards season. After it blew up a sleepy Cannes earlier this year, earning a 20-minute standing ovation, winning a shared best director prize and selling to Netflix , “La Bola Negra” has been an object of fascination across the film world. And since it became the first non-English-language film since 2011 to win the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival, it’s been perceived as the only Oscar contender that might topple “The Odyssey” come March. (“The Odyssey” is a technically dazzling, timeline-toggling examination of the power of love set against the madness of war, while “La Bola Negra” is … also all of those things, just made on a much smaller budget. And for those who consider Los Javis too out of nowhere to get past Nolan — well, who’d heard of the Daniels before they beat Steven Spielberg?)

Which means that these two actors, not yet well-known in the U.S., are about to be everywhere. And that niceness that Almodóvar identified might take Guitarricadelafuente a long way. The singer has a sweetly earnest disposition, with a floaty tendency to remember the emotional truth of working with Los Javis, while Bernardeau is more plainspoken, analytical and forthright, and never once slips into speaking Spanish, even as his co-star lets off soft “Sí”s like punctuation. Together, though, they are comfortable enough to pick up sentences where the other leaves off, and to chuckle — sometimes ruefully, sometimes giddily — while remembering the film shoot that made Guitarricadelafuente an actor, and that changed both their lives.

If the film does score at the Academy Awards, it’ll be a milestone for global cinema, for Netflix and for queer artists: Although Bernardeau doesn’t identify as queer, Guitarricadelafuente is among several out gay actors playing gay characters in the Oscar race, including Andrew Scott of “Elsinore” and Jordan Firstman of “Club Kid.” That makes this year, perhaps, an even gayer Oscar race than the one where “Moonlight” beat a musical, befuddling Faye Dunaway.

But more than 20 years after 2005’s “Brokeback Mountain” won nearly every precursor but lost on Oscar night, are audiences ready for a movie this steamy and provocative? What’s onscreen is potent, so much so that the actors say they had to take care to keep the romance from becoming so overwhelming that it strained credulity. “We had to work against it and try to manage the volume of that love,” Bernardeau says, “because it’s an impossible love.”

Through their efforts, something universal emerges — assuming a post-“Brokeback,” post-“Moonlight” audience is open to it. “Older generations that would have been scandalized by this 20 years ago are gonna understand it right now,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “And this transcends: It’s a story about love that everybody can feel linked to.”

“La Bola Negra” links itself to the audience’s sentiments through deep specificity. It refuses to hold our hand, trusting us to keep up as the work and life story of Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca grow increasingly woven into the text, or when a notification sound from gay sex app Grindr is the cue that first shunts us into modern times. “I don’t like movies that treat me like I’m dumb,” says Calvo, 35, via Zoom during a joint interview with Ambrossi. “The audience is smart enough. When I see ‘Chernobyl,’ I maybe don’t get some nuclear stuff, but I’m in it. In the gay world — no difference.”

In an unprecedented show of confidence, Netflix is giving the film a 47-day theatrical release, starting Oct. 16.

“We made this movie for the screen,” says Ambrossi, 42. “We shot it in 35mm. So that was good news, that people can experience the movie as we thought they would. But Netflix, you can rewatch — you can see all of Penélope Cruz’s numbers again and again.”

“And over and over and over again!” Calvo jumps in.

Netflix’s acquisition deal was announced on the festival’s last day. For a streamer that has earned Oscars — but, frustratingly for its ambitious leadership, never best picture — for films by global cinema stalwarts like Jane Campion, Alfonso Cuarón and Guillermo del Toro, the relative upstarts Los Javis may, surprisingly, represent its best chance yet at Oscar’s top prize. Two years ago, the company bet on a different Cannes prize winner about queerness told in the Spanish language, and the fate “Emilia Pérez” met after lead actress Karla Sofía Gascón’s incendiary old tweets emerged may help account for why team “La Bola Negra” speaks, to a one, thoughtfully and deliberately. The directors are eager to make the leap into being globally known auteurs: Los Javis previously created the biographical TV series “Veneno,” about trans Spanish singer Cristina Ortiz Rodríguez, which aired stateside on HBO Max in 2020. In their home country, they’re famous as judges on “Drag Race España,” and became the subject of speculation over their romantic relationship — they broke up during the making of “La Bola Negra,” but remain creative partners.

Calvo mentions that while both “Brokeback Mountain” and “Moonlight” boosted acceptance of queer love, he hopes that “La Bola Negra,” which is more direct in its depiction of gay sensuality and the male body, can push still further. “There’s no better way to get people to understand things than art and movies,” he says. “They’re a really good vehicle for creating empathy — because when you cry with someone, you’re always bonded to that story, to that person, to that community.”

He sees the change films have made, though, as incremental rather than revolutionary. “Thanks to the work of activists, artists, step by step, it’s a better place. But hate is a shadow that still haunts us.” The success of “La Bola Negra” may indicate something hopeful in our dark historical moment — that a love story, especially a seemingly impossible one, can stop us in our tracks and make us feel.

But to get there, the directors needed to find their perfect leading men. What Almodóvar may have deemed simply nice, Calvo calls “this sad-eyes, little-gay-soldier look” — an easily wounded, fragile quality that had shown through in Guitarricadelafuente’s music. As a singer, he’s collaborated with the Australian pop star Troye Sivan, and, sylphlike and dreamy, he cuts a similar figure, just in the Spanish language; though he hasn’t crossed over stateside, Guitarricadelafuente sells out arenas in Spain.

The singer’s casting also felt political: As a young actor, Calvo played a gay character in the issue-driven teen drama “Física o Química.” “And then nobody hired me anymore,” he says. “People tend to hire straight stars because they don’t want to risk money, which I think is homophobic. We wanted to make this statement.”

The directors approached Guitarricadelafuente at Primavera Sound, a music festival held in Barcelona, where he lives. “You’re saying this because everybody’s drinking right now,” the singer recalls telling them. “You’ve had too many drinks!” The next day, though, Calvo messaged Guitarricadelafuente and asked him to come to Madrid, where Los Javis live. They explained the character they had in mind, one they hadn’t yet started writing but knew was right for him. It was a “Star Is Born” moment — which Guitarricadelafuente has now heard a thousand times.

“Gaga is the exact example that everybody talks to me about!” he laughs. “You’re Lady Gaga! You’re Lady Gaga!” (He relates more to Rosario Flores, a Latin Grammy-winning songstress who appeared in Almodóvar’s “Talk to Her.”) While he was uncertain about acting, his character’s sweetness and connection to music, felt legible to the newly minted actor. “If I was born in that village, in those circumstances,” Guitarricadelafuente says, “that would exactly be me.” Among the points “La Bola Negra” makes is that our contemporary understanding of queerness isn’t a historical constant — that it was learned, and fought for, by people following their hearts despite colossal opposition. A young man in a small town in 1937 might never have realized what lay beyond.

Guitarricadelafuente’s background as a musician only helped make his case to his prospective directors. “All the decisions you take when you’re singing to make things one line louder, one line softer — everything is an acting decision,” Calvo remembers telling him. “So we’ll guide you. We’ve been acting teachers — we know how to work with newcomers.” But Guitarricadelafuente’s scene partner needed to be someone less green. “We couldn’t have two nonactors,” Calvo says. “There’s something interesting in having a wildness in a newcomer that is ready to give all of himself, reminding actors with long careers that they have to let themselves go, and the technique of the professional actors teaching the newcomers.”

Enter Bernardeau, who studied acting in Los Angeles but returned to Spain to find fame on the Netflix teen soap “Elite.” In it, he played the popular stud at an exclusive prep school. The show ran eight seasons, but Bernardeau departed after the fourth. “I learned a lot doing ‘Elite’ about what I wanted and what I didn’t want,” he says. The practice of being on camera on a major production was helpful, he says, but global popularity on a Netflix hit brought tabloid fame. Not every actor wants their Wikipedia to have a “Personal life” section, as Bernardeau’s does.

“What happened later was something that we didn’t expect, and changed our lives and made us reconsider everything,” he says. “I had to protect myself from not getting too busy in what people were saying. It helped me to know what I want — the kind of actor I want to be.”

Bernardeau met Los Javis at the Goya Awards, and they told him that they wanted him to read for them. A week later, he did, and felt he’d botched it. “I woke up every morning and I was like, ‘Please give me another chance.’ Then the casting directors called me again.” At their next meeting, the directors offered Bernardeau the role.

“I hate auditions!” Ambrossi says — he doesn’t even recall that first audition. Los Javis knew they wanted Bernardeau, and the rest was a formality. “We trust ourselves a lot as actors’ directors. It’s what I told Álvaro.” (Guitarricadelafuente’s real name is Álvaro Lafuente Calvo; his grandmother gave him his nickname, which combines “guitarrica,” a diminutive that means “small guitar,” with his surname.) “It’s not your song, but you will have to find a middle point between our text and your voice.”

It had been important to the directors to give an out gay performer a chance to lead their movie. But Bernardeau’s straightness didn’t stand in the way of his being cast. “I totally get why straight actors want to play gay roles,” says Ambrossi. “It’s their craft to portray people that are different from them. I’m not against that. The political statement is still there with the LGBTQ+ people on camera and behind the camera. I guess Miguel is in such a good moment in his career that he wanted a challenge.” Bernardeau’s character, Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, was a real person — an activist and actor who’d been Lorca’s romantic partner before the poet’s 1936 assassination by Franco’s forces, spurring Rodríguez Rapún to fight the fascists. Ambrossi notes that his sexuality was a source of confusion. “Rafael was not an open gay man. He was confused — someone that was not able to say what he wanted.”

For his part, Bernardeau says he felt no doubt whatsoever about playing a gay role, even though, until the last decade or so, many actors shied away from onscreen intimacy with other men. “I never thought about it like that, or cared what people would think about my sexuality,” he says.

Once shooting was underway, Los Javis leaned on the trust they’d built with their leading men during the casting process. Though there are credited intimacy coordinators, “we just worked it out with the Javis,” Bernardeau says.

“ Sí ,” adds Guitarricadelafuente. “I remember Ambrossi saying, Just kiss. Just a little bit more. ” The cast and crew were living in the northern town of Comillas, where they were shooting in an old hospital. They gathered one night in Ambrossi’s kitchen to “go, How are we gonna do this? ” Guitarricadelafuente says. “We wrote the script of what’s going to happen the next day between us — meeting ourselves, thanks to the direction of the Javis.”

“We learned how to be directors doing our thing and learning by ourselves,” Ambrossi says, “so we are super aware how much you need the space to make mistakes, to try new things, to get mistaken. We always wanted to give them that space of freedom.”

Bernardeau had a teen TV-hunk image that he was subverting not just by playing gay but by allowing himself to be objectified by Sebastián. And yet he didn’t feel conflicted about it when shooting a nude scene where his character is recovering from his injuries on an army cot. “I was very comfortable doing everything,” he says, “because I understood exactly what they needed. And they were not like these directors that are on the monitors and have this tent where they’re away. They’re holding your hand, crying with you many times and telling you, Thank you for this .”

It wasn’t just during the love scenes that the directors shed tears. “They cry with you,” Guitarricadelafuente agrees. “When we were preparing the character, I went to Madrid to meet them and to do some acting exercises to reach the emotion — places of your inner self that you didn’t reach before.” He offers an example: Because the innocent Sebastián is deeply connected to his mother, Calvo and Ambrossi asked Guitarricadelafuente to imagine being held in his mother’s arms. On shooting days, they would pull him aside, put on music and discuss what the singer calls “the traumas” — they’d weep, then get ready to shoot.

“There was a very therapeutic thing about it,” Guitarricadelafuente says.

“We cried so many times together.”

Los Javis speak with me the day of the movie’s Toronto debut, and they present a study in contrasts. Ambrossi can’t sit still, and has left his hotel to speed-walk through the city, speaking rapidly and barely glancing at his phone screen. Calvo, meanwhile, sits at a desk in his hotel room, gazing into the camera lens placidly while idly sketching on a sheet of paper.

As we speak, the film’s success at TIFF lies ahead. And waiting doesn’t suit them. Indeed, at Cannes, Calvo sat through the screening in a state of torment. He’d shown up at the theater at 3 a.m. the night before to set the volume. “I was so tired, and I was like, Play it really loud . And then when we were there, I was like, I think I put it too loud . Javi was like, Shut up! Let me enjoy it! ” It was only after the movie ended that Calvo dialed back into the experience, and began to cry.

Ambrossi is accustomed to micromanaging — because he’s always had to. “The posters, the merchandising, calling networks — Please, I need more money — I’m very used to that. So this movie — everything was very hard. It was the biggest effort I ever made.” So Cannes provided a moment of serenity. “I felt peaceful, and it was a new feeling for me to feel peaceful. I saw Tilda Swinton’s face in the next row — Oh my God, what’s happening? ”

Diva worship is a thread that connects the ex-lovers: Calvo gravely corrects my statement that, between Cannes and “Drag Race España,” the pair toggle between high and low culture. “For me,” he intones, “drag is high art.” For their part, the stars of “La Bola Negra” marvel at their directors’ varied interests. “I think it would be cool to have Christopher Nolan as a ‘Drag Race’ juror,” Bernardeau says. “Woody Allen!” Guitarricadelafuente fires back drily.

Calvo uses drag-club slang to describe Cruz’s character, Nené Romero — “She is mothering!” he says. Nené is a cupletista , a Spanish singer whose bawdy, openly sexual acts were inspired by the goings-on at the Moulin Rouge. “They talked about sex, drugs, all the experiences in the street, and they were friends with gay and lesbian writers. They were the first pop stars you get in Spain,” Calvo says. Cruz’s performance — which has, despite its brevity, sparked Oscar chatter, and which might, along with her work in Olivia Wilde’s “The Invite,” make her the first performer to get two nominations in one category under the Academy’s new rules — recalls Liza Minnelli’s in “Cabaret.” Minnelli’s Sally Bowles lived loud and hard in the last days before Weimar Berlin fell to Adolf Hitler. On the precipice of Franco’s dictatorship, Cruz’s character is doing the same.

Nené — outrageous and drag-inflected — opens Sebastián up to the power of queerness, and Cruz played a similar role for Guitarricadelafuente. “She was a godmother in every single aspect,” Ambrossi says. “Guitarricadelafuente, she took such care of him. But she was so generous — she wanted to support the message of this movie and the importance of the political statement behind it.”

“She was so generous and gentle and trying to encourage you,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “This poor guy in the middle of the civil war, this beautiful show is the first time you see him smiling. And her role in this is very important, because she’s going to be a mother for a lot of queer people that are going to see this.” Guitarricadelafuente notes that Nené seems to intuit that about his sexuality that Sebastián cannot yet put into words. “She’s like the English teacher who encourages you to see beautiful things — she already knows. She knows before you know.”

In the midst of telling a story about self-discovery and new love, Los Javis transitioned from romantic and creative partners to solely creative partners. Endlessly protective of their actors, they kept their breakup under wraps during the shoot.

“I didn’t even notice,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “I noticed after we ended filming.”

“They told me on my last day,” says Bernardeau.

Guitarricadelafuente didn’t want to believe the news, despite gossip swirling around the production. “There was like a fuss, because they are very known in Spain,” he says. “I was like, I’m having dinner with them every day, and they’re so close.”

Today the directors are philosophical about their split. “When we get into a project, it’s a road to the unknown,” says Calvo, “and we always trust that by the end of the road, we are going to be different people.”

“Yeah!” interjects Ambrossi.

“And that’s the good thing about doing what we do,” Calvo says. “The way I see creation is: You can’t make a project that is not going to change your life forever, and I was grateful for this project to make us evolve and make us explore new ways of living.”

This evolution happened at the moment the pair’s stature on the film scene was about to shift, first with Cannes and possibly again next March. But they’re not allowing themselves to think as far ahead as the Oscars, even as Netflix, with “La Bola Negra” as the crown jewel in its 2026 slate, clearly is.

“Javi Ambrossi — I think he’s a witch. Not a witch, but he has a spiritual thing. He knows things about the future, and he’s not telling us,” Guitarricadelafuente says.

“And his phrase is always ‘Step by step, step by step,’” Bernardeau adds. “And you’re like, ‘Step by step’?! These are big leaps!”

Ambrossi learned this incrementalism from moviemaking. He used to be an actor, too, and becoming a director — with so many tasks competing for his attention all at once — was terrifying until he simplified the process for himself. “You have to go frame by frame — it’s the only way to do things,” he says. “Day by day, frame by frame. You do your best every single second, and it will be OK. Today is the Toronto premiere. Hopefully, people will connect. We’ll see tomorrow.”

For his part, Calvo emphasizes the film’s potential impact — illuminating a story of queer hope during a dark stretch of history, then as now. His ambitions reach beyond the Oscar race. Academy attention, he says, “would be a dream come true, but you should remember why you made the movie. Making the movie was a dream. Everything is a dream. So we just keep dreaming.”

article_text:
Julia Stiles ’ tribute to her “10 Things I Hate About You” co-star Heath Ledger on “ Dancing With the Stars ” next week is sure to be a teary-eyed performance.

“I was crying in rehearsals today,” Stiles told me Thursday at the InStyle Imagemaker Awards in Los Angeles. “It’s so crazy.”

It was revealed earlier this week that Stiles and her professional partner Ezra Sosa will perform to Frankie Valli’s 1967 song “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” during “DWTS” Dedication Night. In “10 Things I Hate About You,” Ledger’s character serenades Stiles with the song.

Related Stories

Fueled by ‘La Bola Negra,' Spain’s Indie Distribution Make Robust Gains, to Be Highlighted at Valladolid's Merci Market

Serielizados Prizes: Hagai Levi’s ‘Etty' and 'Astonishing' ‘Killing a Bear’ Win Big as ‘El Observatorio' Bags the Mind the Gap Pitch Prize

“I know that Dedication Night is emotional, but I thought I was distanced from it enough. Like, oh, it was so many years ago,” Stiles said. “Something about seeing clips from that movie and images and hearing my voice and hearing his voice is bringing back so many memories. It’s a lot.”

I asked Julia last night how rehearsals were coming along. https://t.co/42HtNrSMoh via @variety #justforvariety #redcarpet pic.twitter.com/fkRSigdoRu — Marc Malkin (@marcmalkin) October 16, 2026

Dedication Night airs on ABC on Oct. 20.

“One of the things that I’m taking away from this dedication is one of the things that we really hope to do as performers is to make people feel something and have people care about the work that you do, and his memory lives on because it was such an incredible performance,” Stiles said.

Stiles also said that “DWTS” producers had asked her to compete on the show for the past couple of years before she finally agreed to do it.

“I think it was turning 45,” she explained. “I was like, ‘I’m halfway to 90! Why not? It’s now or never.’ I knew that there were going to be emotional hurdles that I’m going to have to get over on this show, like getting over my own nerves, finding my love of performing again, being able to dance in front of an audience, all these things.”

And then Stiles deadpanned, “I was like, ‘Yeah, maybe I should tackle that in front of millions and millions of people.’”

title_original: Frieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent
editorial_title_zh: Frieze 艺术展评论——你在《烘焙大赛》（Bake Off）的帐篷里都能看到更多前卫的奇观
editorial_excerpt_zh: 伦敦摄政公园 今年的艺术博览会是一场面向超级富豪的平庸画作旧货甩卖，而它的姊妹展“大师展”（Masters）则在兜售恐龙头骨和庸俗的19世纪人体画。欢迎来到最怪诞的艺术市场 裸体的人从地下爬出来，四处奔跑……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "光着身子的人从地下爬出来，挥舞着手臂尖叫，同时一个长着鸟头和翅膀的人在吹风笛。这是今年 Frieze 艺术展上我最喜欢的艺术品，但你可别指望在 Frieze 伦敦展（Frieze London）堆积如山的当代艺术中寻找这种极富想象力的离奇之作。这是一幅16th世纪耶罗尼米斯·博斯（Hieronymus Bosch）追随者的画作，正在 Frieze 大师展（Frieze Masters）上展出，那是摄政公园另一侧更显高档的帐篷。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我很遗憾地说，我在 Frieze 伦敦展上感到无聊至极。我想，许多人来这里是希望能从最新、最酷的艺术中获得启发和兴奋，但你在《烘焙大赛》的帐篷里都能看到更多真正前卫的奇观。这里有无穷无尽的画作，没有一幅算得上优秀，其间穿插着往往要好一些的照片。这里第一件稍微吸引我的东西是沃尔夫冈·蒂尔曼斯（Wolfgang Tillmans）创作的一幅高2米的喷墨印刷作品，名为《保罗，裸体，高尔夫球》（Paul, nude, golf ball），画面中赤裸的保罗双肘撑地，修剪整齐的头部低垂在双肘之间，流露出显而易见的绝望，而他身旁白色的高尔夫球则诡异地呼应着他那骨感背部的苍白肤色。但这并不是新作——它的创作时间可追溯到1994年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还有，天哪，那些画作。似乎有成百万幅之多。而一个摆满画廊展位的优雅白色大帐篷，夹在无尽的白色走廊里，是展示它们的糟糕方式，也是观看它们的恐怖方式。这远不如参观那些本身就是有趣空间的画廊来得有回报。在这里，一切都被塞得满满当当，就像一家巨大的商店——艺术界的塞尔福里奇百货公司（Selfridges）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d4e4cf594f55f4dc4db97bd5ab96180994fc9d4a/0_152_7307_4559/master/7307.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "2026年 Frieze 伦敦展上的施特鲁特·玛格斯（Spruth Magers）展位。", "caption": "“艺术界的塞尔福里奇百货公司”……2026年 Frieze 伦敦展上的施特鲁特·玛格斯（Spruth Magers）展位。摄影：Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/Frieze", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据称，Frieze 定义了新事物并寻找明日之星。但显而易见，它真正服务的是卖家的需求和某种极度富有消费者的品味。这一点在VIP日表现得最为明显，当时我与一大群科技兄弟、对冲基金经理、退休对冲基金经理、他们的孩子以及——那是乔治·奥斯本（George Osborne）吗？——一同入场，他们实际上就是来买这些东西的。在 Frieze 大师展上，我正要询问一件表面覆满缠结枯枝的安塞尔姆·基弗（Anselm Kiefer）作品的价格，一对老年夫妇却抢在我前面问了。他们是真的有兴趣购买。价格略低于100万英镑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你可以挂在墙上的东西依然是最具收藏价值的艺术。在 Frieze 大师展上，你会找到已确立地位的现代“大师”的作品，其中许多人已经去世：サイ・トゥオンブリー（Cy Twombly）的一系列带有涂鸦污渍的视觉诗篇，莱昂·科索夫（Leon Kossoff）的一幅灰暗、凄凉的裸体画。但在当代艺术展上，有些作品简直是旧货甩卖的水准。在洛杉矶的“夜间画廊”（Night Gallery）展位上，旺达·库普（Wanda Koop）的《光芒-共生》（Radiance-Together）描绘了两根蜡烛在蓝紫色背景下并排燃烧。啊，真可爱。到底谁会把这当回事？它的另一位艺术家安迪·沃尔（Andy Woll）展示了一排笔触懒散的山景，同样空洞无物。与此同时，在名副其实的格林画廊（Grimm Gallery），以电影闻名的罗莎琳·纳沙什比（Rosalind Nashashibi）展出了一幅平庸的情侣画，背景夹在繁花边框之间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在，这里有些不一样的——一排白色矿物般的生长物，诡异的美丽，带有神秘的有机感：它们是海伦·查德威克（Helen Chadwick）的《尿液之花》（Piss Flowers），这是拥有这位在1996年去世的伟大艺术家的现代经典作品的机会。为什么她没有去 Frieze 大师展那边呢？在埃德尔·阿桑蒂（Edel Assanti）展位的后方，则是朗尼·霍利（Lonnie Holley）的装置作品：一个固定在缠绕着铁丝的生锈水管上的水龙头，以及粗糙木底座上的两个绿玻璃瓶。它带有现实生活的粗砺质感。霍利是一位来自阿拉巴马州伯明翰的音乐家兼艺术家，几年前他展示了自己如何能用一截随意的铁丝创造出美感，曾让我着迷不已，他是这个平庸世界中脱颖而出的真正的美国伟大艺术家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "“一场失去理智的资本主义盛会”……2026年 Frieze 伦敦展上的高古轩（Gagosian）展位。摄影：Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/Frieze", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "特拉西·艾敏（Tracey Emin）、瓦卡斯·汗（Waqas Khan）、徐道获（Do Ho Suh）、凯瑟琳·奥皮（Catherine Opie）和扎内尔·穆霍利（Zanele Muholi）也是如此——但平心而论，Frieze London 的成功率大约只有 10 分之一。对于一个声称能定义艺术时代精神的活动来说，这个比例实在太低了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而在 Frieze Masters，你拥有现存最好的品质证明：时间。如果某样东西在经过50、500或68,000,000年后依然保有价值，那它大概率是件好东西。这68m年绝非夸张，因为这里正在出售一具带有三只角的化石三角龙头骨。这难不成真的会沦为某个有钱人家里的装饰品吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让我们客观来看。把这个头骨称为“博物馆级”都算是一种保守的说法。自然历史博物馆也没有拥有如此完美的三角龙化石。正如《卫报》最近报道的那样，古生物学家们担心，超富阶层中风靡恐龙标本的风气正在推高价格，将博物馆拒之门部门外。这里正在出售好几个这样的奇珍。", "links": [{"text": "as the Guardian recently reported", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/science/audio/2026/aug/18/ultra-rich-collecting-fossils-bad-for-science-podcast"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/49447921c14c45d02d8442386042c59386494916/0_373_4724_2749/master/4724.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Frieze 大师展上待售的头骨。", "caption": "“更加丰盛、奇特”……Frieze 大师展上待售的头骨。摄影：Hugo Glendinning/ Frieze", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frieze 大师展在视觉上比 Frieze 伦敦展更令人兴奋。它更丰盛，也更奇特。你可以买到盔甲、银器、阿拉伯地毯——一个颓废的唯美主义者在1896年可能会用以环绕自身的物品。这让你意识到当代艺术展是多么因循守旧。在 Frieze 大师展上，你可以放纵你最反常的品味——这里有大量低俗的19世纪人体画。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但它在更有趣的同时，也更加令人反感。各个展位将历史物件顶礼膜拜，把它们剥离出各自的语境，当作明亮耀眼的玩意儿来展示：从抄本上割下来的手稿页、古埃及棺木上的面具、公元2世纪帕尔米拉的祭司石雕头像。这些东西本该属于博物馆，但它们却全都齐聚于此，沐浴在奢侈与金钱那孤立的聚光灯下。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一场彻底失控的资本主义盛宴。我可以开玩笑说你可能会买这个或那个，但你不会，除非你是个亿万富翁，我亦不会。安迪·伯纳姆（Andy Burnham）之前是怎么说的来着？关于新自由主义的暴政。在这里，它在商品化的狂热狂欢中扭曲了艺术。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Colnaghi 的展位简直就像是为艺术市场量身定制的马克思主义揭露现场。非洲木雕立在一幅贾科莫·格罗斯（Giacomo Grosso）创作于1920年的媚俗裸体画前。画面中，模特躺在丝绸上，其臀部的奢华视角以及她脚踩高跟鞋的细节，滑稽而又赤裸裸地表明这是一幅精工细作的软色情作品。而那些为宗教目的而创作的非洲艺术，在这个商品化的躯体衬托下被贬低成了装饰品。约翰·伯格（John Berger）这位激进的评论家曾将裸体画及其他形式的商品化艺术视为西方资本主义的玩物，他大概会说：我早就说过吧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "艺术", "links": [{"text": "Art", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/art"}], article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "N aked people climb out of the earth and run around waving their arms and screaming, while someone with a bird’s head and wings plays the bagpipes. It’s my favourite artwork at this year’s Frieze but don’t go looking for this wildly imaginative outrage among the heaps of contemporary art at Frieze London. It’s a painting by a 16th-century follower of Hieronymus Bosch and is on view at Frieze Masters, the posher tent on the other side of Regent’s Park."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I’m sorry to say I was bored rigid in Frieze London. Many people attend, I imagine, hoping to be informed and excited by the newest, coolest art, but you’ll see more genuinely avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent. There are endless paintings, none of which are much good, interspersed with photographs which tend to be a little better. The first thing here that held me at all was a two-metre-tall, inkjet print by Wolfgang Tillmans called Paul, nude, golf ball in which the naked Paul has his elbows on the floor and his close-cropped head bowed between them in apparent despair, while the white ball beside him eerily mirrors the pale flesh of his bony back. But it’s not new – it dates from 1994."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And, oh Lord, those paintings. There seem to be millions of them. And an elegant white marquee full of gallery booths along endless white corridors is a ghastly way of showing them, a dreadful way of seeing. It’s not as rewarding as visiting galleries which can be interesting spaces. Here, everything is crammed in, like a huge shop – the Selfridges of art."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d4e4cf594f55f4dc4db97bd5ab96180994fc9d4a/0_152_7307_4559/master/7307.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Spruth Magers stand at Frieze London, 2026.", "caption": "‘The Selfridges of art’ … Spruth Magers stand at Frieze London, 2026. Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/Frieze", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frieze, it is claimed, defines the new and finds the stars of tomorrow. But it’s obvious that it really serves the needs of sellers and the tastes of a certain kind of extremely wealthy consumer. This is most apparent on VIP day when I enter along with a host of tech bros, hedge-fund managers, retired hedge-fund managers, their children, and – is that George Osborne? – who were actually here to buy this stuff. At Frieze Masters, I was about to ask the price of an Anselm Kiefer work, matted vegetation clogging its surface, when an elderly couple beat me to it. They were genuinely interested in purchasing. The price was just shy of a million quid."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Things you can put on your wall are still the most collectible art. At Frieze Masters, you will find works by established modern “masters”, many of whom are deceased: a series of stained, graffiti-laden visual poems by Cy Twombly, a grey, bleak nude by Leon Kossoff. But at the contemporary fair, some of it is jumble sale standard. At Los Angeles’ Night Gallery booth, Wanda Koop’s Radiance-Together depicts two candles burning side by side in a blue and purple setting. Aw, cute. Who on earth would take this seriously? Another of its artists, Andy Woll, shows a row of lazily brushed mountain views that are just as vacuous. Meanwhile, at the appropriately named Grimm Gallery, Rosalind Nashashibi – better known for her films – exhibits a silly painting of lovers between flowery borders."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Now here’s something different – a row of white mineral-like growths, eerily lovely, enigmatically organic: they’re Helen Chadwick’s Piss Flowers, a chance to own examples of a modern classic by this tremendous artist who died in 1996. Why is she not over in Frieze Masters? And at the back of the Edel Assanti booth is Lonnie Holley’s assemblage of a water tap on a rusty pipe entwined with wire and two green bottles on a rough wooden plinth. It has the raw tang of real life. Holley, a musician and artist from Birmingham, Alabama who held me spellbound a couple of years ago when he showed how he can create beauty from a random piece of wire, is a true American great who stands out in this blandfest."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/55d76f9969ccb5bb659468e1e44b24b7f03b7c96/42_0_2462_1717/master/2462.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Gagosian stand at Frieze London, 2026.", "caption": "‘A festival of capitalism run amok’ … Gagosian stand at Frieze London, 2026. Photograph: Linda Nylind/Linda Nylind/Frieze", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So do Tracey Emin, Waqas Khan, Do Ho Suh, Catherine Opie and Zanele Muholi – but in all honesty the success rate at Frieze London is about one in 10. That’s far too low for an event claiming to define the artistic zeitgeist."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Over at Frieze Masters, you’ve got the best certificate of quality there is: time. If something has value after 50, 500, or 68,000,000 years, it’s probably good. That 68m years is no exaggeration for here on sale is a triple-horned, fossilised Triceratops skull. Is this really going to end up as decoration in some rich dude’s house?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Let’s get it in perspective. To call this head “museum quality” is an understatement. The Natural History Museum does not own a Triceratops fossil of this perfection. Palaeontologists, as the Guardian recently reported , are worried that the fashion for dinosaur specimens among the ultra-rich is inflating prices and locking out museums. There are several such marvels being sold here.", "links": [{"text": "as the Guardian recently reported", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/science/audio/2026/aug/18/ultra-rich-collecting-fossils-bad-for-science-podcast"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/49447921c14c45d02d8442386042c59386494916/0_373_4724_2749/master/4724.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A skull for sale at Frieze Masters.", "caption": "‘Fruitier, stranger’ … a skull for sale at Frieze Masters. Photograph: Hugo Glendinning/ Frieze", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frieze Masters is more visually exciting than Frieze London. It’s fruitier, stranger. You can buy armour, silverware, Arabian carpets, the stuff a decadent aesthete might have surrounded themselves with in 1896. It makes you realise how conformist the contemporary fair is. At Frieze Masters, you can indulge your most perverse tastes – there are loads of sleazy, 19th-century nudes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But if it is more interesting, it is also more disgusting. Stalls fetishise objects from the past, ripping them out of context to display them as brightly lit gewgaws: a manuscript page cut from its codex, a face mask off an ancient Egyptian coffin, a stone head of a priest from 2nd century AD Palmyra. These things belong in museums, but here they all are in the isolating spotlight of luxury and money."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is a festival of capitalism run amok. I could say jokingly you might buy this or that but you won’t, unless you are a squillionaire, nor will I. What was it Andy Burnham was saying about the tyranny of neoliberalism? Here it distorts art in a delirious orgy of commodification."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Colnaghi booth could have been designed as a Marxist exposé of the art market. African wooden carvings stand in front of a kitsch 1920 nude by Giacomo Grosso. article_text:
N aked people climb out of the earth and run around waving their arms and screaming, while someone with a bird’s head and wings plays the bagpipes. It’s my favourite artwork at this year’s Frieze but don’t go looking for this wildly imaginative outrage among the heaps of contemporary art at Frieze London. It’s a painting by a 16th-century follower of Hieronymus Bosch and is on view at Frieze Masters, the posher tent on the other side of Regent’s Park.

I’m sorry to say I was bored rigid in Frieze London. Many people attend, I imagine, hoping to be informed and excited by the newest, coolest art, but you’ll see more genuinely avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent. There are endless paintings, none of which are much good, interspersed with photographs which tend to be a little better. The first thing here that held me at all was a two-metre-tall, inkjet print by Wolfgang Tillmans called Paul, nude, golf ball in which the naked Paul has his elbows on the floor and his close-cropped head bowed between them in apparent despair, while the white ball beside him eerily mirrors the pale flesh of his bony back. But it’s not new – it dates from 1994.

And, oh Lord, those paintings. There seem to be millions of them. And an elegant white marquee full of gallery booths along endless white corridors is a ghastly way of showing them, a dreadful way of seeing. It’s not as rewarding as visiting galleries which can be interesting spaces. Here, everything is crammed in, like a huge shop – the Selfridges of art.

Frieze, it is claimed, defines the new and finds the stars of tomorrow. But it’s obvious that it really serves the needs of sellers and the tastes of a certain kind of extremely wealthy consumer. This is most apparent on VIP day when I enter along with a host of tech bros, hedge-fund managers, retired hedge-fund managers, their children, and – is that George Osborne? – who were actually here to buy this stuff. At Frieze Masters, I was about to ask the price of an Anselm Kiefer work, matted vegetation clogging its surface, when an elderly couple beat me to it. They were genuinely interested in purchasing. The price was just shy of a million quid.

Things you can put on your wall are still the most collectible art. At Frieze Masters, you will find works by established modern “masters”, many of whom are deceased: a series of stained, graffiti-laden visual poems by Cy Twombly, a grey, bleak nude by Leon Kossoff. But at the contemporary fair, some of it is jumble sale standard. At Los Angeles’ Night Gallery booth, Wanda Koop’s Radiance-Together depicts two candles burning side by side in a blue and purple setting. Aw, cute. Who on earth would take this seriously? Another of its artists, Andy Woll, shows a row of lazily brushed mountain views that are just as vacuous. Meanwhile, at the appropriately named Grimm Gallery, Rosalind Nashashibi – better known for her films – exhibits a silly painting of lovers between flowery borders.

Now here’s something different – a row of white mineral-like growths, eerily lovely, enigmatically organic: they’re Helen Chadwick’s Piss Flowers, a chance to own examples of a modern classic by this tremendous artist who died in 1996. Why is she not over in Frieze Masters? And at the back of the Edel Assanti booth is Lonnie Holley’s assemblage of a water tap on a rusty pipe entwined with wire and two green bottles on a rough wooden plinth. It has the raw tang of real life. Holley, a musician and artist from Birmingham, Alabama who held me spellbound a couple of years ago when he showed how he can create beauty from a random piece of wire, is a true American great who stands out in this blandfest.

So do Tracey Emin, Waqas Khan, Do Ho Suh, Catherine Opie and Zanele Muholi – but in all honesty the success rate at Frieze London is about one in 10. That’s far too low for an event claiming to define the artistic zeitgeist.

Over at Frieze Masters, you’ve got the best certificate of quality there is: time. If something has value after 50, 500, or 68,000,000 years, it’s probably good. That 68m years is no exaggeration for here on sale is a triple-horned, fossilised Triceratops skull. Is this really going to end up as decoration in some rich dude’s house?

Let’s get it in perspective. To call this head “museum quality” is an understatement. The Natural History Museum does not own a Triceratops fossil of this perfection. Palaeontologists, as the Guardian recently reported , are worried that the fashion for dinosaur specimens among the ultra-rich is inflating prices and locking out museums. There are several such marvels being sold here.

Frieze Masters is more visually exciting than Frieze London. It’s fruitier, stranger. You can buy armour, silverware, Arabian carpets, the stuff a decadent aesthete might have surrounded themselves with in 1896. It makes you realise how conformist the contemporary fair is. At Frieze Masters, you can indulge your most perverse tastes – there are loads of sleazy, 19th-century nudes.

But if it is more interesting, it is also more disgusting. Stalls fetishise objects from the past, ripping them out of context to display them as brightly lit gewgaws: a manuscript page cut from its codex, a face mask off an ancient Egyptian coffin, a stone head of a priest from 2nd century AD Palmyra. These things belong in museums, but here they all are in the isolating spotlight of luxury and money.

This is a festival of capitalism run amok. I could say jokingly you might buy this or that but you won’t, unless you are a squillionaire, nor will I. What was it Andy Burnham was saying about the tyranny of neoliberalism? Here it distorts art in a delirious orgy of commodification.

The Colnaghi booth could have been designed as a Marxist exposé of the art market. African wooden carvings stand in front of a kitsch 1920 nude by Giacomo Grosso. The lavish view of the model’s bum as she lies on silks and the fact that she’s wearing high heels make it comically clear this is finely painted soft porn. The African art, made for religious purposes, is reduced to decor in front of this commodified body. John Berger, the radical critic who saw nude paintings and other forms of commodified art as playthings of western capitalism, might have said: told you so.

article_text:
With DC’s Clayface in theaters this weekend and Marvel’s Avengers: Doomsday barreling toward us, users online have been playing compare/contrast.

One commenter apparently had questions about the connectivity between the projects in the DC Cinematic Universe being created by James Gunn and Peter Safran. Listing six recent projects — Superman , the Peacemaker series, Supergirl , the animated Creature Commandos , Clayface and the much-lauded series Lanterns — the person is question asks, “What’s this building towards??????”

Related Stories

‘Clayface’ Scares Off Elizabeth Holmes & Nathan Fielder From No. 1 With $24M; But ‘You Can See Everything’ Still Widely Seen With Near Epic $20M – Update

Peter Safran Still “Confident” In DCU Strategy After ‘Supergirl’ Didn’t Meet “Box Office Expectations”

Reposting that comment on Threads, an account called lostuslandcomics replied, “Gunn doesn’t have to build towards anything if the individual pieces work on their own…I think the MCU reprogrammed people’s expectations.”

Watch on Deadline

Gunn commented over the weekend, “I couldn’t agree more. DCU is just an alternate universe; we can enter at any location or time and tell THAT story. I dislike the idea that individual stories aren’t meaningful unless they lead to something else.”

The co-CEO of DC Studios went on to point out that “Star Wars has essentially been doing this for 50 years across movies, shows, games and books.” He added that his Superman Saga — which continues with next year’s Man of Tomorrow — “contains many characters we’ve introduced in other stories. But that doesn’t mean those other stories only exist to set up what’s happening there.” (Marvel might argue that that “only exist” bit is a little reductive.)

He ended with, “I would love people to be seeing ‘Clayface’ because it’s a great, fun horror movie unto itself, not because of where else Clayface will show up three movies from now.”

Here is Gunn’s reply in full:

I couldn’t agree more. DCU is just an alternate universe; we can enter at any location or time and tell THAT story. I dislike the idea that individual stories aren’t meaningful unless they lead to something else. People not understanding this is strange to me, because Star Wars has essentially been doing this for 50 years across movies, shows, games and books, admittedly without the tonal variety. Now, this doesn’t mean there isn’t connectivity.

The Superman Saga starts with Superman and travels into Man of Tomorrow and onward, and contains many characters we’ve introduced in other stories. But that doesn’t mean those other stories only exist to set up what’s happening there. I would love people to be seeing ‘Clayface’ because it’s a great, fun horror movie unto itself, not because of where else Clayface will show up three movies from now.
