article_text:
La Gradiva sort en pleine mobilisation lycéenne, et son jeune casting est de tous les fronts : plusieurs acteur·ices ont défilé samedi dernier sous l’oeil de Libération. Et trois comédie·n·es (Colas Quignard, Suzanne Gérin et Mitia Capellier-Audat) ont profité de l’exposition du plateau de Quotidien pour porter la parole de la jeunesse.Mais que dit vraiment ce film de la génération qui lutte ?

Sans jamais tomber dans l’effet catalogue, le premier long métrage de Marine Atlan saisit les sentiments mêlés de l’adolescence d’aujourd’hui, son bouillonnement, mais aussi son anxiété face à un avenir qui semble bouché. Dans le film, cette parole prend encore plus d’ampleur face au vertige des vestiges millénaires de Pompéi.

« J’ai réécrit en fonction des acteurs, de ce qu’ils apportaient. Ils ont été d’une intelligence émotionnelle incroyable, très bienveillants entre eux, très à l’écoute. Rien n’était laissé de côté. Personne n’était abandonné », nous confiait Marine Atlan en mai dernier, à Cannes, à propos de son casting d’acteur·ices non professionnel·les.

« Pour certaines scènes, comme celle qui se passe dans la chambre des filles, on écrivait des dialogues, puis on en parlait avec eux ou elles. Je voulais qu’il y ait de l’ambivalence, que les points de vue se contredisent, que rien ne soit figé. »

Gustave, un des acteurs du film, confirme à Libération , qui a suivi une partie du casting venue manifester à Paris samedi dernier : « On s’est vus sept fois pendant un an […]. La volonté de Marine était qu’il n’y ait aucun figurant, chacun avait un personnage à part entière. On a eu ces débats sur l’égalité des chances, les moyens donnés aux profs… Et encore, dans le film, le dialogue est possible. Moi, j’étudie à Lille, il y a des méga fafs, les divisions sont plus violentes. »

Cette volonté d’inclure la jeunesse dans l’écriture du film a conduit Marine Atlan à réécrire des dialogues, mais aussi à redessiner certains profils pour éviter les stéréotypes. Mitia Capellier-Audat, qui joue James (un adolescent au charme ténébreux), en témoigne à Libération : « Quand Marine m’a proposé le rôle, elle m’a dit que c’était un BCBG, j’ai dit : ‘’c’est quoi ça ?’’ Le personnage est devenu moins cliché, politisé, plus fou sur les normes de genre. » Pour lui, La Gradiva est le « film pré-révolte » d’une jeunesse qui a battu le pavé contre la mort de Nahel, la réforme des retraites, ou pour la Palestine. Sur le plateau de Quotidien , l’acteur raconte avoir été repéré par la directrice de casting… en manif.

« Quand on sent la porosité, l’écho, la caisse de résonance que peut être le cinéma, c’est très réjouissant », nous a confié Antonia Buresi, que l’on a rencontrée plusieurs jours avant la manifestation . « Tout à coup, il y a une espèce de prise de relais avec le réel, qui permet que les discussions autour du film puissent agir au présent . »

L’actrice incarne Madame Mercier, une professeure passionnée qui revendique une pédagogie axée sur le dialogue et l’horizontalité entre élèves et professeurs.

« Dans le film, il y a l’évocation de Parcoursup, mais aussi celle des conditions d’un système éducatif qui n’est pas réformé depuis des décennies. […] Ça traduit non seulement un état de fait concret, matériel, mais aussi une appréhension d’un monde angoissant, et leur besoin, à un moment donné, de se situer et de prendre part. C’est ça aussi, l’initiation . »

Elle précise : « Les questions de rapports de domination, de pouvoir, la question du genre, la fluidité : il y a quelque chose qui s’est intégré, incorporé, qui a été pris en main par cette nouvelle génération, avec des outils qui leur permettent d’agir, et pas juste de les manipuler comme des concepts. Donc plutôt que de se dire que cette jeunesse est juste abêtie devant des réseaux et ne sait pas discerner le vrai du faux avec les fake news , là, on voit qu’on a une jeunesse active et déterminée. »

La Gradiva de Marine Atlan, en salles depuis le 21 octobre

article_text:
Michael Douglas reached his limit playing Hank Pym (the original Ant-Man ) after two Marvel movies, but the studio refused to grant him his wish when he asked for the character to be killed off. The Oscar winner was asked during a recent “Happy Sad Confused” interview if the stories were true about him wanting to be killed off from the Marvel Cinematic Universe, to which he responded: “I would have been killed off after the second one, but they wouldn’t let me.”

Related Stories

ABC Orders Drama Pilot 'Rabbit' Based on U.K. Series 'Ludwig' From Megan Ganz & Humphrey Ker

Elizabeth Banks Officially Set to Play Karen Read in Amazon Series

Appearing on “The View” in 2024, Douglas said he asked Marvel to kill him off in the third standalone “Ant-Man” movie, “Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania,” and even pitched an idea of how to do it that included a special effects bonanza.

“[Getting killed off] actually was my request for the third one,” Douglas said at the time. “I said I’d like to have a serious [death], with all these great special effects. There’s got to be some fantastic way where I can shrink to an ant size and explode, whatever it is. I want to use all those effects. But that was on the last one. Now, I don’t think I’m going to show up [for a fourth].”

Douglas debuted as Hank Pym in 2015’s “Ant-Man” and returned in three follow-up appearances: 2018’s “Ant-Man and the Wasp,” 2019’s “Avengers: Endgame” and 2023’s “Quantumania.”

“I said, ‘I’ve never done a green screen movie,’” Douglas said on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast about wanting to join Marvel “I [told] all my agents, ‘I’d like to do one of these green screen movies to see what they’re like,’ you know? Because it’s amazing. It’s nothing, just a green screen and they show you the pictures of what it’s gonna look like when it’s all finished.”

“It’s hard acting, man,” he added. “It’s coming at you here, this and that, you know… We did ‘Ant-Man’ and Paul Rudd was a wonderful actor — a lovely group — but then you can’t get out of it.”

article_text:
Tokyo has a reputation for its immaculate, orderly streets, but Kenya Sugai’s snapshots reveal a city littered with broken objects, accidental spills, eerie shadows, and stray reflections. “I tend to look at the world a bit cynically,” the photographer tells me. “I’ve always been drawn to society’s errors, like someone tripping over, or strange situations that come about by chance.” Sugai has been building this archive of crude coincidences for over ten years, cataloging them year by year on his website in a list simply titled “Portfolio A.”

Like his images, Sugai carries a wayward energy. Born in Kyoto in 1977 but raised in the southern city of Fukuoka, he found himself lost after high school. His parents were fed up with him “drifting around,” so they sent him to study in London. During his introductory film studies, he presented some of his street photography and a tutor pointed him to Martin Parr’s book Common Sense (1999), which had just been released that year. “It had a real impact on me,” Sugai says. “It showed me the kind of expression that was possible as a street photographer.” Parr led him to William Eggleston, then to Paul Graham, Richard Misrach, and other photographers of the New Color Photography movement. When Canon’s Shashin Shinseiki award invited Parr to be a judge several years later, Sugai entered the competition. An honorable mention gave him the confidence to pursue photography as a career.

Sugai’s current style of shooting—direct strobe paired with abrupt, disjunctive cropping—started to emerge after that, as he began to feel the limits of the traditional snapshot, which he viewed as too reactive and dependent on chance. “It just wasn’t interesting to me anymore,” he says. “I wanted to figure out how I could bring my own expression into it.”

He began to practice a daily “personal training exercise” that has stuck for over a decade. This involves roaming high-traffic areas of his local ward, Setagaya, mostly the four-lane Route 246 or the Kanpachi and Kannana ring roads. He limits himself to just ten to twenty pictures a day.

The resulting images are at once abrasive and strangely seductive—a clash of beauty and ugliness frozen by an unforgiving flash. Humans are only briefly alluded to, as half-torsos, blurred reflections, or a spill on the sidewalk, while the city’s best-dressed pets—bichon frisés, giant poodles, and chihuahuas among them—make frequent cameos. At times, the collection feels more like a catalog of the city’s textures: polished steel, rusted iron, and corrugated shutters, shot with and in between browning bushes and roots of trees breaking through the pavement. The series is still ongoing, but the photographer is now compiling all existing images into a publication titled First Decade Report .

“Over the years, as I kept shooting and selecting, the social meaning of the subjects, and my interest in that meaning, gradually faded,” he says. “I started to lose track of details like where I took a photo. . . . The sense of distance, of time, of the situational context all started to dissolve. I began to realize I wasn’t photographing the scene itself, but simply my own perception of it.”

He offers an analogy: “When we are newborns, the first things we see are just colors and shapes, with no distinction between, say, a person or a cup. . . . There’s no social understanding yet. I want to see things that way as much as possible.”

Read more from our series “ Introducing ,” which highlights exciting new voices in photography.
excerpt_original: From giant poodles to accidental spills, Kenya Sugai finds strange pleasures among the city’s shadows.

article_text:
ヨーロッパ貴族所有、ブルガリの24カラット・ピンクダイヤモンドリングが初競売へ。最高28億円予想

不純元素をほとんど含まない非常に希少な24カラット・ビンクダイヤモンドの指輪が、 クリスティーズ の オークション に出品される。1950年代に ブルガリ で製作され、由緒ある貴族が所有していたもので、オークションに登場するのは初めて。

11月10日、ジュネーブで行われる クリスティーズ の「マグニフィセント・ジュエルズ（絢爛たる宝石）」 オークション に、 ブルガリ が1950年代に製作した伝説の「ファンシー・インテンス・ピンク（彩度が非常に高いピンク）」ダイヤモンドの指輪が出品される。同オークションはオータム・ラグジュアリー・ウィークの一環として開催されるもので、指輪の予想落札価格は1200万から1800万ドル（約19億〜28億円）。

プレスリリースによると、24カラットのピンクダイヤモンドは現在の所有者の曽祖父がインドで入手したもので、1950年代に ローマ を本拠地とするブルガリに指輪の製作が依頼された。70年以上にわたりこの指輪を所有していたのは、「由緒あるヨーロッパの貴族の家系」とされ、オークションへの出品は初となる。

世界的な高級宝飾品ブランドのブルガリは、19世紀の創業以来ローマを本拠地としている。ローマは、第2次世界大戦の敗戦後に新生イタリア共和国の中心として復興し、指輪が製作された1950年代には賑わいを取り戻していた。その華やかさについて、プレスリリースでは次のように述べられている。

「ハリウッドの大作映画の数々がチネチッタ・スタジオで撮影され、世界的なスターたちが集まったローマは、『テヴェレ川のほとりのハリウッド』と呼ばれるようになった。コンドッティ通りにあるブルガリのブティックは社交や文化交流の場となり、 エリザベス・テイラー とリチャード・バートン夫妻、オードリー・ヘプバーンとメル・ファーラー夫妻といった大物カップルや、各国の著名なセレブを数多く顧客として抱えていた」

今回出品されるダイヤモンドは、窒素やホウ素などの不純元素をほとんど含まない「IIaタイプ」に分類されている。これは全世界の天然ダイヤモンドのうち2％未満しか存在しない非常に希少なもので、その色合いは「coveted fancy pink（垂涎の的のファンシーピンク）」と形容される。

米フォーブス誌の 報道 によると、独特のピンク色は「地球内部での形成過程で非常に強い圧力が加わることによってダイヤモンドの結晶格子に希有な歪みが生じ、この構造的変形がダイヤモンドを透過する光の進み方を変える」ことによって生み出されるという。（翻訳：石井佳子）

article_text:
Lee Friedlander, Maria and Erik, New City, New York , 1961

Reviews - October 9, 2026

Piper French

Lee and Maria Friedlander recount the beginning of their long life together in much the same way. After running into her at the Sports Illustrated offices, where she worked as an assistant—women weren’t allowed to write for the magazine in 1958—Lee called Maria up and asked her to a Count Basie show at the jazz club Birdland. “I went and—it never stopped,” she told the gallerist Jeffrey Fraenkel in 2019. In Lee’s telling, they went to see Basie—“And that was it.” First date, rest of life. They have now been married sixty-eight years.

For each of those years, Lee has taken portraits of his wife: Maria caught in profile; Maria by Lee’s side; Maria holding their infant son; Maria at the wheel; Maria dozing off in the grass; Maria in Paris, Santa Fe, or Wales; Maria doing the crossword with their now adult daughter; Maria reading the funny pages with her daughter’s young son.

Wales , 1992

Maria and Giancarlo, New City , 2001

The photographs, currently on display at San Francisco’s Fraenkel Gallery, are clearly “Friedlanders.” They have a formal rigor to them. They are all monochrome. Lee, the original selfie king, is often present—sometimes only obliquely, his shadow stamped onto Maria; always in the clarity of his vision. But these pictures are also more intimate than much of Lee’s work. A 1974 photograph taken on a camping trip in Colorado is an apt spatial rendering of the family dynamic, with its uneasy miasma of romantic and domestic love. In the right half of the image, the couple’s children occupy themselves at the picnic table; on its left, Maria, in dishabille, meets Lee’s gaze from the back of the camper, a look of sly complicity creasing her face. These portraits document the relentless etchings of time: Maria’s cheeks hollow; a furrow appears in her forehead; her mane of black hair lightens and one day reappears cropped short. Later images of her reclining, legs splayed, or reviewing documents in her underwear are discomfiting, and forceful, in their rare combination of aging, eroticism, and the mundane.

Maria, New City, New York , 1971

The word muse does not seem quite right here: Lee felt the compulsion to make photographs long before he met Maria, and he would have gone on doing so if there had been no Sports Illustrated encounter, no Basie show. (“What’s in front of me starts to get photographed. And Maria has been in front of me a lot,” he told one interviewer, characteristically unsentimental.) But his portraits evince a steady desire to keep looking and an awareness of what they cannot see, two qualities that seem essential to the tenacity of a marriage. Consider Maria’s appraisal of why their sometimes troubled relationship endured: “No matter what was going on, we always did what we said we were going to do.” “I’m certainly curious about Maria,” Lee said, more than thirty years in. “I still am.”

Maria, Las Vegas , 1970

In some of these images, Maria revels in Lee’s gaze, preening like a rock star or a fashion icon; in others, she seems to reluctantly tolerate it, or merely looks back at him, inscrutable. Who knows what she’s thinking? She has compared the experience of looking back at Lee’s pictures of their shared past to “rereading a private journal.” Unlike Lee, who is often comically taciturn when asked about his work, Maria’s essays and interviews allow us a degree of access into that hidden world. They reveal a life not merely documented by her husband’s camera but also molded by it. She recalls her discomfort, in the years after his late ’70s Nudes series, when women they knew socially would brazenly ask him to shoot them naked. Photographs Lee took in 1979 of a then unknown Madonna later put their children through college; Lee and Maria went to the theater to see Desperately Seeking Susan and realized that his former nude model was now a famous singer and actress. Other luminaries appear, at decidedly human scale. (Maria is drily hilarious on the topic of Garry Winogrand, Lee’s contemporary: “Garry seemed happy as he said his third ‘I do’”; “Garry never punched anyone in our house.”) Lee made his first portrait of Maria with Walker Evans’s camera.

New City, New York , 1962

All photographs © the artist and courtesy Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco and Luhring Augustine, New York

Maria’s Shadow, New City, New York , 2012

Maria has written about the emotional whiplash of seeing the arc of her family’s life represented in book form. The passage of decades can seem to collapse in on itself: There she and Lee are with their young children, and a few pages later, those same children have grown up and are holding babies of their own. Fraenkel’s visual presentation achieves the same effect. The photographs on the main wall of the gallery balloon outward in the fullness of midlife, then taper. The final portrait shows the couple’s shadows, shoulders touching. You feel the weight of life and its ephemerality; the endless span of days, weeks, months, and the speed with which, looking back, it has vanished.

In 2019, when Fraenkel interviewed Maria for a Friedlander retrospective, she spoke bluntly about the vicissitudes of old age. Her eyesight was failing, robbing her of “one of the greatest pleasures of my life.” Lee, meanwhile, had whittled down the substance of his own life, retreating into his work: “The darkroom has become his cupola.” Nearly everything has gone, but Lee and Maria are still there, together. And so is Lee’s camera.
excerpt_original: For nearly seventy years, Lee and Maria Friedlander have shared a bond shaped—and at times distorted—by photography.

At a swanky restaurant in LA, four people aglow with self-importance embark on the time-honored ritual of discussing the screenplays they’re working on – specifically, the screenplay Martin (David Schwimmer), is “working on”. It’s classic industry navel-gazing, underscored by a tight focus on Martin’s clammy face as he sputters poorly through a confidence game."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Schwimmer, of course, is still best known for playing a perpetually and comedically exasperated sitcom character; it’s hard to square that extremely familiar voice with Martin’s dark bluster on how “drug-addled gen Zers” have “no respect for the communal aspect of the cinema”, an off-putting rant that is also a tad intriguing – who is more pretentious here, the sweaty character or the picture starkly sending him up?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But Junk, directed by Jack Begert from a script co-written with Dani Goffstein, swerves quickly and, for too long, inexplicably to a different stratum of Hollywood. article_text:
Y ou could be forgiven, upon watching the first scene of Junk, for believing that this debut feature will boldly, perhaps ill-advisedly, dare to satirize the industry it’s purporting to join. At a swanky restaurant in LA, four people aglow with self-importance embark on the time-honored ritual of discussing the screenplays they’re working on – specifically, the screenplay Martin (David Schwimmer), is “working on”. It’s classic industry navel-gazing, underscored by a tight focus on Martin’s clammy face as he sputters poorly through a confidence game.

Schwimmer, of course, is still best known for playing a perpetually and comedically exasperated sitcom character; it’s hard to square that extremely familiar voice with Martin’s dark bluster on how “drug-addled gen Zers” have “no respect for the communal aspect of the cinema”, an off-putting rant that is also a tad intriguing – who is more pretentious here, the sweaty character or the picture starkly sending him up?

But Junk, directed by Jack Begert from a script co-written with Dani Goffstein, swerves quickly and, for too long, inexplicably to a different stratum of Hollywood. Somewhere else in the city, two burnouts, played by Dominic Fike and Talia Ryder, find themselves without their car, pills or plans once a house robbery goes awry. The sharp pivot is confusing, though not unwelcome; Begert, a prolific director of surrealist music videos for artists such as Olivia Rodrigo , Doja Cat and Kendrick Lamar, has an eye for LA’s seedy beauty, the way a night can unwind like the city’s endless roads. You could, like the chihuahua nicked from the house and hot potatoed while the thieves flee to the scene to the modest synths of Caroline Polachek’s So Hot You’re Hurting My Feelings, just be along for the ride.

Alas, it’s a bumpy and unsatisfying one. Junk is molded from another feature by a different name, Little Death, that premiered at the Sundance film festival back in 2024. According to press notes, that earlier movie was “a different shape entirely” from the new picture released by Mubi , though “at heart it’s the same movie.” I unfortunately missed Little Death on its festival run, where it picked up a Sundance innovator award, so I cannot speak to what, exactly, has changed, though the new shape is an odd one: two loosely connected stories of addiction and desperation in LA, one far more compelling and visually stimulating than the other, and only one deserving the film’s billing as a “slacker odyssey” across the city.

That section, as AJ (Fike) and Karla (Ryder) struggle to score and strive in nearly equal measure, beguilingly conveys, for a too brief stretch, the feeling of an unplanned evening in LA, hazy and sprawling and peopled by unpredictable characters who are at once assertive and stoned. There’s something appealing, if derivative, to lurking with two kids as they hurdle roadblock after roadblock of their own making. The appearance of Euphoria alum Fike, as another optimistic addict endearing even as he’s lying through his teeth, recalls the audacity of that now-cursed show – an impression unfortunately underscored by a visit to an antiseptic, sinister apartment owned by a drug dealer with “school shooter vibes” (an off-putting Karl Glusman) that undercuts the film’s woozy naturalism.

Unfortunate, too, that the 110-minute film’s middle section returns to Schwimmer’s screenwriter, sweatily withdrawing into fantasy with a molten core of self-loathing. The title card, presented 35 minutes in, presents an art exhibit that teases Junk as “a search for meaning in the post-post-modern dilemma” – a line surely meant as a joke, though it more or less describes the film’s grating meta ambitions, as Martin maybe or maybe not writes the other half of the story. It is, I assume, supposed to be ironic that Martin, stymied by a male protagonist deemed too “unlikable” by broadly drawn film executives, resorts to increasingly repellant behavior and flights of fancy. But whatever the intentions (and impressive flourishes of surrealist animation), it is certainly a slog to witness. The fact that, in taking the exec’s notes that he switch his protagonist to a woman in order to get made, Martin is played, for a time, by Gaby Hoffman, scans as unduly cynical. (And the less that is said about a recurring fantasy sequence involving a beautiful woman, played by Angela Sarafyan, in a barn described by his therapist as his “mother’s womb”, the better.) That Jena Malone, as Martin’s beleaguered fiancee, gets a well-earned tirade puncturing his absorption is only fair, though of little comfort.

If this sounds like the review of two entirely different movies – well, though connections between the two are eventually revealed, Junk never coheres into one picture. There’s admirable ambition here, and plenty of sumptuous visuals to spare, but the clash between one section’s biting cynicism and another’s ragged heart proves too discordant to overcome. Which is a shame; as a whole, the film may be a mess, but there are little treasures within this Junk to perhaps be reimagined down the road.

article_text:
Art Movements

Studio Museum Announces New Artists-in-Residence

Plus, this year's Prix Duchamp winners, a trove of Kiki Smith prints heads to NYPL, and more.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Studio Museum in Harlem Names Three Artists-in-Residence

Multidisciplinary artist Turiya Adkins , artist and curator Timothy Yanick Hunter , and photographer and filmmaker Clifford Prince King have been selected as the Studio Museum’s yearlong artists-in-residence for 2026–27. Starting this November and through October 2027, the three will have individual studio spaces in the institution's new building on West 125th Street. The residency also includes professional development training and material support, and culminates with a group exhibition in one of the museum's galleries. (An exhibition of the latest cohort’s work is currently on view through January 3.)

Brognon Rollin Wins Prix Duchamp

The Prix Duchamp, France's largest contemporary art award, goes this year to Brognon Rollin , the artist duo formed by David Brognon and Stéphanie Rollin . Winners receive a €35,000 (~$39,200) prize and participate in an exhibition of works by all four nominees, now on view through February 7 at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris. The museum’s director, Fabrice Hergott , praised Brognon Rollin’s conceptual practice as “a quiet yet tenacious statement on human vulnerability,” adding that their work “gives tangible form to what usually escapes our gaze: the passage of time spent waiting, addiction and inner resilience.”

Joël Andrianomearisoa , Laura Henno , and Josèfa Ntjam were also nominated for the award this year.

What Else Happened?

Queer|Art, the Bronx Council on the Arts, A.I.R. Gallery, and Visual AIDS are among the 59 nonprofit art organizations receiving grants from the New York State Council on the Arts (NYSCA) and the New York Foundation for the Arts. The NYSCA Reserve Fund Grants range from $15,000 to $50,000 and total $1,760,000 in support; see all grantees here .

Anthea M. Hartig , director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, has been elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

Americans for the Arts named Matt Ryan as chief operating officer and Cillonia McKenley as chief development officer.

Patrick Eugène is now represented by Vielmetter Los Angeles.

Rachel Kanter and Yana Peel were appointed to the Yale Schwarzman Center’s advisory board.

Acquisitions

The New York Public Library (NYPL) is the lucky recipient of 250 prints by Kiki Smith , one more fantastic and exquisite than the next. Rich hand-colored intaglios, woodcuts, and artists’ books are part of the trove gifted by her sister, artist Seton Smith , which comprises the most comprehensive collection of Kiki Smith’s prints in the United States. In a statement, Kiki Smith said that she “could think of no more wonderful place for my prints to be.”

The Cleveland Museum of Art announced today the acquisition of Teresita Fernández ’s “Soil Horizon (Cleveland)” (2026), a site-specific commission consisting of two large-scale glazed ceramic wall murals. The piece will be on view in the museum’s Jane and Jon Outcalt Family Concourse beginning in February.

Wildcard

Seaworld Venice by artist Florentina Holzinger for the 61st Venice Biennale (photo Giuseppe Cottini/Getty Images)

For the coda to Seaworld Venice , Florentina Holzinger ’s installation for the Austrian Pavilion at this year's Venice Biennale, the artist will present a “final dinner” featuring all the bodily waste collected from visitors over the past seven months. “Closing Étude” at the Scuola Grande della Misericordia in Venice will extend the pavilion's central conceit, which involved filtering urine from on-site port-a-potties into a dunk tank. The “distilled remains serve as a monument for the future” that will be presented outside the closed pavilion on November 22, a statement explains. Okay!

article_text:
Drawing on Afrofuturism, African mythology and the speculative world of Drexciya, ‘From the Deep’ transforms the ocean into a space of ancestral memory, resistance and imagined futures.

What if the Atlantic Ocean, a site of profound historical trauma, could become a space for imagining alternative Black futures? In ‘From the Deep: In the Wake of Drexciya ‘ , American artist Ayana V. Jackson reimagines the histories of the transatlantic slave trade through photography, immersive video, animation and installation. Presented at the Museum of Anthropology in Vancouver, the exhibition marks its Canadian premiere after debuting at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African Art in 2023.

Inspired by Detroit techno duo Drexciya’s imagined underwater civilisation, Jackson constructs a feminist, Pan-African world inhabited by water spirits drawn from African and Afro-Atlantic traditions. Through elaborate costumes, layered soundscapes and underwater imagery, Jackson challenges the historical representation of Black bodies, particularly women, while exploring the possibilities of mythology and speculative storytelling as forms of cultural reclamation. Moving between historical violence and imagined liberation, the exhibition considers how the legacies of the Middle Passage continue to shape diasporic identity and collective memory.

Rather than allowing the Atlantic to remain defined solely by loss, Jackson transforms its depths into a site of possibility, where ancestral histories are reconsidered, and new narratives of survival, belonging and freedom emerge.

This exhibition will be on view at the Museum of Anthropology, University of British Columbia in Vancouver , from 19 November 2026 to 29 March 2027.

Sponsored

Louis Grandchamp des Raux Collection: A shared Modernity

MAURICE DENIS (1870–1943),

L’Île Chevalier , 1894. Estimate: EUR 700,000–1,000,000.

Presented by ArtCurial

On October 24, 2026, during Art Basel Paris , Artcurial will auction Louis Grandchamp des Raux’s collection , A shared Modernity . Bringing together nearly 75 works by 44 artists, this remarkably cohesive collection reflects a discerning and sensitive eye, shaped over twenty years of passionate collecting.

Spanning the major movements that transformed French and Belgian painting from the late 19th to the mid-20th century, the collection traces a journey from Impressionism to Symbolism, from the Pont-Aven School to the Nabis, and ultimately to the chromatic freedom of Bonnard. More than a historical panorama, it reveals the personal affinities of a collector drawn to artists who helped redefine painting and usher it into modernity.

The Conquest of Modernity

The collection opens with the pioneers of plein-air painting and Pre-Impressionism, including Théodore Géricault’s Cheval alezan and Jean-François Millet’s Barque de pêche , estimated at €500,000–800,000. Corot, Courbet, and Boudin further illustrate the growing sensitivity to nature, light, and the painted motif that would pave the way for the revolutions of the second half of the 19th century.

JEAN-FRANÇOIS MILLET (1874–1875),

Barque de pêche , circa 1870-1871. Estimate: €500,000 – 800,000.

THÉODORE GÉRICAULT ,

Cheval palomino effrayé par un lion et une lionne, 1822–1823. Estimate: €350,000 – 450,000.

Impressionism is represented by two paintings by Berthe Morisot, Dans les vignes and La Roche Plate au Portrieux (est. €200,000–300,000), whose delicate brushwork captures the fleeting effects of light. Works by Henri Martin, Armand Guillaumin, and Henry Moret further explore the relationship between landscape and colour.

Dans les vignes , 1882. Estimate : €250,000 – 350,000.

The Pont-Aven School & the Nabis: The Heart of the Collection

At the heart of the collection are the artists who radically transformed the language of painting at the end of the 19th century. The Pont-Aven School and the Nabis are represented by major works by Maurice Denis, Pierre Bonnard, and Édouard Vuillard.

Among the highlights of the sale, Maurice Denis’s L’île Chevalier , estimated at €700,000–1,000,000, stands as the collection’s star lot. It is presented alongside Sancta Martha (est. €600,000–800,000), revealing the spiritual, decorative, and deeply modern dimensions of Denis’s art.

Pierre Bonnard is represented by two works of remarkable chromatic intensity: La petite fenêtre (est. €550,000–750,000) and La baignade (est. €150,000–250,000). In Bonnard’s work, colour becomes an experience in itself, transforming both space and perception and embodying the freedom that characterises his artistic language.

PIERRE BONNARD (1867–1947),

La petite Fenêtre , 1946. Estimate: €550,000–750,000.

Édouard Vuillard’s Misia Natanson dans les bois (est. €450,000–650,000) brings a more intimate dimension to the collection. His subtle interplay of figures, patterns, and surroundings blurs the boundaries between portrait, interior, and decorative composition.

Vallotton, Laval, Sérusier, and Paul Ranson, with Suzanne et les vieillards , further enrich this exceptional chapter devoted to one of the most fertile periods in the development of modern painting.

Belle Époque & Symbolism: Worlds Within

The collection also explores the more mysterious and introspective worlds of the Belle Époque and Symbolism. Louis Anquetin’s Au bar , alongside works by Forain and Raffaëlli, evokes the nightlife and social fringes of a Paris in full transformation.

Belgian Symbolism is represented by two particularly rare works: Fernand Khnopff’s Étude pour la Défiance (est. €300,000–400,000), imbued with an atmosphere of aristocratic melancholy, and Léon Spilliaert’s striking Fillette au grand chapeau (est. €300,000–400,000). Both reveal the Symbolist fascination with introspection, ambiguity, and the world of dreams.

Works by Odilon Redon, Puvis de Chavannes, Lévy-Dhurmer, and Lacoste complete this exploration of an art turned towards the imagination and inner life.

LÉON SPILLIAERT (1881–1946),

Fillette au grand chapeau, bord de mer, 1909. Estimate: €300,000–400,000.

Louis Grandchamp des Raux: A Collector’s Journey

Behind the collection lies a deeply personal story. Louis Grandchamp des Raux began visiting Parisian museums at the age of ten, developing an early and intimate relationship with art. The inheritance of his grandfather’s collection would later crystallise his vocation and sharpen his eye, guided by a simple conviction: to look at a painting as one gets to know a person.

For nearly twenty years, he built a collection devoted to major French painters of the 17th and 18th centuries, including Boucher, Fragonard, Hubert Robert, and Greuze. From 2010 onwards, his focus shifted towards the transition to modernity, from Corot to the Nabis, with a particular fascination for Maurice Denis and Édouard Vuillard and the aesthetic rupture they embodied at the turn of the century.

ÉDOUARD VUILLARD (1868–1940),

Misia Natanson dans un bois , circa 1897-1899. Estimate: €450,000–650,000.

In 2015, the first auction of his collection, dedicated to 17th- and 18th-century French painting and organised with Artcurial and Sotheby’s, marked an important milestone in his collecting journey.

Today, A shared Modernity , continues this dynamic approach to collecting. Rather than allowing a collection to become static, Louis Grandchamp des Raux embraces renewal, guided by passion, high standards, and an ever-evolving eye.

Through this selection, Artcurial presents not only an exceptional group of works, but also the portrait of a collector and his personal journey through the birth of modernity — a modernity he has chosen to explore, share, and now pass on.

For more information, please visit https://www.artcurial.com/en/sales/6540
